prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Some people search because they want out of pain. 'Rock bottom' and 'no hope left' and 'how do I quit drinking' are all someone screaming to escape a situation that is destroying them. Others search because someone they love is watching. 'Affecting their son' and 'be there for his kids and wife' are about protecting the people who count most.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start where they actually are. They aren't looking for a polished program. They're on Day 1, or they are back on Day 1 again, and they feel completely alone. Meet them there.
prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'just quit' and 'you can do this' more times than they can count, and they've tried, and they've slipped in the first week, and that slip felt like proof they're broken. They're not looking for another promise that sobriety fixes everything, because they've quit before and felt lonelier than when they were drinking. What they haven't found yet is something that deals with the part nobody talks about: who they are and who they're with when the alcohol is gone.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop drinking and then build a real life around being sober. Not just white-knuckle it. Actually feel like themselves again, keep the people they love, and not fall back into old patterns.
prose_plain.push: Their drinking has hurt people they love, brought them close to losing everything, and put them within reach of consequences they can't undo.
prose_plain.pull: They believe sobriety opens a better life, and they hold onto other people's encouragement and the idea that there are real things to do and feel instead of drinking.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they'll lose their social life completely, that loneliness and depression are just what sober feels like, and that stopping drinking means losing a version of themselves they can't replace.
prose_plain.habit: They've leaned on alcohol to feel comfortable around other people for so long that stopping feels like showing up to every situation without any armour, and the first few days go fine until something social or stressful breaks the streak.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're standing at what feels like rock bottom and the only thing that cuts through is hearing from someone who stood in the exact same place, because it makes them feel like they're not uniquely broken. When someone in that same spot says 'I'm new here' out loud, it's a small commitment that's hard to walk back from, and that public step keeps them returning. Being seen as part of a group who gets it, not lectured at by someone who never lived it, is what makes them stay.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: People in this market want to protect the people they love. They're yelling at their kids and they hate themselves for it. The guilt hits right after the anger does. Then the stress builds and the whole thing starts again. That cycle is what hurts most, not just the anger itself.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the cycle: anger, then guilt, then the fear of becoming a parent your kids are scared of. Say that out loud before you offer anything practical. People need to feel seen before they trust you enough to listen.
prose_plain.implication: They've already heard 'count to ten' and 'take a breath before you respond.' They tried it and it didn't hold when the moment hit fast. So they're not looking for another tip list, they're looking for something that explains why they snap before they even think, and why the guilt afterward doesn't stop them from doing it again.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop yelling, especially at their kids. Not just in one moment, but for good. So the guilt stops. So they can feel like the parent they actually want to be.
prose_plain.push: They're caught in the same loop of snapping, feeling terrible about it, and then doing it again, and it's tearing them up.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel their anger without it flying out at the people they love most.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this is just who they are, that it's hardwired into their personality or their mental health, and that no amount of work will actually change it.
prose_plain.habit: They apologise after every blowup, they mean it every time, and then they find themselves doing it again before the week is out.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel shame about this, so they don't trust just anyone with it. They need to believe the person helping them actually understands anger at this level, not just stress management in general. And when they see another parent who was stuck in the same yell-apologise-repeat loop and got out of it, that's the thing that makes them believe it's possible for them too.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Your clients are scared, not just stressed. They say things like 'I can't stop feeling anxious', 'I can't breathe', 'I can't focus on anything'. What they want most is simple: feel safe again and get through their day.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by telling them you understand it never switches off. Acknowledge that 'why won't it just go away' feeling before you say anything about how you help. If you skip that, they won't trust the rest.
prose_plain.implication: They've been handed breathing exercises, journaling prompts, and calming routines more times than they can count. They do the things, they get through the day, and then the anxiety comes back anyway, which has taught them that coping tools don't actually fix anything. They're not looking for another technique to try; they want someone to explain why it keeps coming back after everything they've already done.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They aren't looking to feel slightly better. They want the constant anxiety to stop so they can think straight and get on with their life.
prose_plain.push: The anxiety has gotten worse and they can't focus on the basic things their day needs from them.
prose_plain.pull: They don't want to manage anxiety anymore; they want it gone.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid nothing will actually work because they already cope and the anxiety stays anyway.
prose_plain.habit: They white-knuckle through each day with coping strategies that keep the symptoms from peaking but never break the loop that keeps bringing it back.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're scared and they've already been let down, so they won't trust a voice that sounds like it's selling something. They need someone who sounds like they actually understand what's happening inside the anxious brain, because that credibility is the only thing that makes a new explanation feel worth hearing. And when they see that other people who felt exactly this stuck have found real relief, it's the closest thing to proof they can get before they're willing to try again.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Everything in this market points to romantic relationships. People want a relationship that works, or they want to stop hurting over one that ended. The pain they talk about most is the anxious-avoidant cycle and the grief of a breakup they can't let go of.
prose_plain.lead_with: These buyers already know the words. They've taken the quiz. They know if they're anxious or fearful-avoidant. So don't teach them the basics. Start with their exact pairing and give them a clear next step or decision. That's what gets their attention.
prose_plain.implication: They've taken every quiz, read every explainer, and can name their attachment style fluently. They've been told that awareness is the first step, and they took it, but nothing changed in the actual relationship. They don't need another label or another framework explained to them; they need proof that the pattern itself can move.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to understand their own style and their partner's, then either turn the relationship around or make peace with the fact that it's over.
prose_plain.push: They're stuck in a loop where the anxious chasing and the avoidant pulling away feed each other, and sometimes the person they love uses guilt or control to keep them in it, which makes leaving feel impossible and staying feel unbearable.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know whether someone with their exact pairing ever made it work, and if not, they want to know how people who've been through it actually got over the person they still love.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that their attachment style, or their partner's, is just how they're built, and that no amount of understanding it will stop them from ending up in the same place again.
prose_plain.habit: They keep diagnosing themselves and the people they date instead of doing anything that changes how they actually behave when they're triggered.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're skeptical of coaches who just repeat the theory back at them, so they need to see that someone genuinely knows the clinical side before they'll listen. But knowing the theory isn't enough on its own, because they've already read the books. What tips them is finding someone who has been an anxious type or dated an avoidant and got through it, because that's the only evidence they trust that change is real.

prose_plain.implication: They've already tried piecing it together from blog posts, YouTube rabbit holes, and whatever Reddit threads showed up first. A list that looks crowd-tested feels safer than one person's opinion. prose_plain.lf8_evidence: For people with bipolar disorder, staying alive and staying housed isn't a metaphor. It's the actual goal. A manic episode can cost someone their job. Losing a job can mean losing the roof over their head. When they say 'I have to survive', they mean it literally. Security and a stable place to live are what they are fighting for every day.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they have bipolar disorder. They're probably already on medication and seeing someone. Don't start there. Start with the part nobody has helped them with yet: how to hold a job, keep a relationship, and have a normal life on top of the treatment they are already doing.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told that medication plus therapy is the answer, and a lot of them are already doing both. The standard promise didn't stop them from losing a job or a relationship during an episode, so they don't believe the headline anymore. What they're looking for now is something more specific than 'get help' because they already got the help and the hard parts still happened.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Hold my life together, keep a job, relationships, and stability, while managing an unpredictable mood disorder
prose_plain.push: They lost a job during a manic episode and they cycle between rage and a complete flatness that feels like nothing, and that cycling keeps pulling the floor out from under them.
prose_plain.pull: They want to put their life back together while the disorder is still happening, not after it's somehow fixed, because they know it isn't going to be fixed.
prose_plain.anxiety: They believe the world moves too fast and forgives too little, and that stable functioning is something other people get to have but not them.
prose_plain.habit: They manage crisis by crisis, doing whatever gets them through the current episode, without anything in place to see the next one coming before it takes something from them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel like the world is built for people whose moods behave, so seeing someone with bipolar who actually holds a job and keeps relationships is the most convincing thing possible. It shrinks the hopelessness before anything else does. They also want clinical credibility because this is a serious medical condition and they've been burned by oversimplified advice before, so authority signals that whoever is talking actually understands what they're dealing with.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Fear of the cancer coming back runs through almost everything these buyers say. Survival and relief from that fear are what they want most. They say it plainly: constant worry, anxiety after diagnosis, dread that it will return.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the fear they live with every day: what happens after chemo ends, and how lost and scared life feels once treatment is over. Then tell them a normal life is possible again. That's what gets their attention.
prose_plain.implication: They've been handed pamphlets, told to 'stay positive', and sent home after treatment like the hard part is over. The medical system marked them as done, but they don't feel done. They've heard that anxiety is normal and time heals it, and neither of those things has been true for them.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me stop being afraid the cancer will come back and let me feel normal and enjoy my life again.
prose_plain.push: They're stuck in a limbo where chemo is over but life hasn't started again, and the fear of recurrence runs in the background of every single day like an alarm that won't shut off.
prose_plain.pull: They want to watch a movie, plan a holiday, laugh with people they love, and feel like someone who just happens to have had cancer rather than someone who's still in it.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that the moment they stop worrying and watching, that's exactly when the cancer comes back, so the vigilance feels like the only thing keeping them safe.
prose_plain.habit: They stay locked in high-alert mode and some of them have reached for medication just to quiet the noise in their head, because that feels more manageable than trusting that it's actually okay to feel okay.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust someone who hasn't felt what they've felt, so they buy from people they genuinely like and believe actually get it. They need to see other survivors who moved past the fear because they can't yet imagine it's possible for themselves. And because this sits right next to their medical care, the coach has to feel credible enough to deserve a seat at that table.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These people feel torn in two. On one side, they love their parent and feel it is their duty to show up. On the other side, caregiving has cost them real things: a marriage, a house, their own sense of who they are. When they ask 'how do I have a life?', that isn't a small question. It's a cry for basic comfort and normality. Add in conflict with siblings or a spouse and they are also scared of being judged by the people closest to them.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by calling out the exact pain they are living with: the burnout, the resentment, the feeling that the person they used to be has gone, the fights with family. Then say out loud that wanting a life of your own isn't selfish. Say it clearly, before you say anything else. They need to hear that first. Only then do you talk about what you can do for them.
prose_plain.implication: Most of what they've found talks about the parent's wellbeing, the parent's dignity, the parent's needs. They've heard plenty about how to be a better caregiver and almost nothing about how to stay a whole person while doing it. So they've learned to assume that any help on offer is really just more pressure to give more.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to care for their ageing parent without it destroying their marriage, their finances, their health, or their sense of who they are.
prose_plain.push: Caregiving has already cost them their marriage, their financial stability, and their sense of who they are.
prose_plain.pull: They want a way to stay in their parent's life and still have a life of their own.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that drawing any line means they're selfish, ungrateful, or will blow the family apart.
prose_plain.habit: They keep over-giving because stopping feels like abandonment, and that feeling is strong enough to overrule everything else.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel profoundly alone in this, like admitting they're struggling makes them a bad child, so when someone speaks as a fellow caregiver rather than an expert looking down, they relax and listen. They're not looking for a system, they're looking for someone who gets it without judging them. And because guilt is running the show, they won't give themselves permission to set a limit unless someone they trust tells them it's okay to do it.

prose_plain.lead_with: Start with what they feel in the moment: the shaking voice, the blank mind, the freeze. Then promise that they can feel calm even when a presentation is coming up fast.
prose_plain.implication: They've already read the tips, done the breathing exercises, and practiced in the mirror. They walked into the room prepared and their body still betrayed them, so they don't believe confidence advice works for people like them. What they haven't seen yet is someone who can explain why the physical freeze and shake happen and show them how to stop it at the source.

prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that nothing will actually help, because they prepared and practiced before and their body still locked up on them.
prose_plain.habit: They stay quiet unless someone directly asks them something, and when they can't avoid speaking they over-prepare in ways that don't stop the freeze when it hits.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're frightened and they've already failed with generic advice, so they won't trust just anyone. prose_plain.lf8_evidence: People in this market say things like 'I feel like an empty shell', 'I feel numb', 'I can't go on anymore', and 'I spend most of my day in bed crying'. That tells you the pain is raw and serious. They aren't looking to improve their life. They're looking to survive it.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by meeting them where they are. Acknowledge the numbness. Acknowledge the emptiness. Answer the question they are really asking: 'Can I get back to normal?' Give them hope and make them feel seen. Don't open with what your program includes.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to talk about it, to open up, to reach out, and they did those things and still feel like an empty shell. The standard advice hasn't moved anything for them, so they've stopped believing that words, on their own, are going to change how they feel. They're not cynical by nature, they're just tired of being promised relief that didn't come.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to feel something again. And they want to believe that a normal life is still possible after what they have been through.
prose_plain.push: They feel like an empty shell, numb, and like they can't go on anymore.
prose_plain.pull: They're holding onto the hope that normal life is still possible and that they can feel like themselves again.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that what they're feeling is permanent and that severe depression is simply too far gone to fix.
prose_plain.habit: They stay in bed and withdraw from everything, and they've built up a strong belief that talking won't help, which makes them less likely to reach out and more likely to stay isolated.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're in a place where they genuinely can't picture getting better, so hearing from someone who felt exactly what they feel and came through it is the only thing that makes hope feel real rather than hollow. They don't trust encouragement from people who haven't been there, so unity and social proof aren't nice-to-haves, they're what cracks the door open. A coach who can show real badges also helps, because part of what keeps them stuck is the belief that their depression is too severe for anything to touch it.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: When your clients say things like "my mind gets clouded and I snowball into negativity" or "I self-soothe with food", they are telling you they want relief from pain above everything else. They aren't chasing a goal. They're trying to stop hurting. The fact that they name it as a restrictive eating disorder and talk about years of struggle tells you they see this as a health issue, not a lifestyle tweak.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the binge-restrict cycle and the habit of reaching for food when feelings get hard. They already know this pattern. They live it. Lead with the relief they want, not another diet. Diets are what already failed them.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to eat less, track more, and try harder, and they did try, more than once, for years. Every time a diet worked briefly and then they binged and the shame hit harder than before. They don't trust promises about food freedom because every promise so far has just restarted the same cycle.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me stop bingeing and reaching for food every time I feel bad, so I can feel in control and stop the shame spiral that comes after.
prose_plain.push: After six-plus years of trying, they keep going back to food when things get hard, and every binge pulls them into a negativity spiral they can't think their way out of.
prose_plain.pull: They want to reach a point where a hard day doesn't end in a binge, where food is just food and the shame doesn't follow.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this really is just a self-control problem, and that since every diet has failed them so far, nothing else will work either.
prose_plain.habit: When distress hits, they reach for food to feel better, and when the guilt follows they go back to strict rules, which sets the whole thing off again.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They already blame themselves for having no willpower, so they need someone who can explain clearly why restriction made the bingeing worse, not because they were weak but because the cycle itself caused it. They also need to see real people who looked exactly like them and got out of it, because without that proof they assume they're the one person it won't work for.

They also respond to small, concrete steps because finishing each one proves to themselves they're actually changing.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These buyers are scared. They use words like 'froze', 'mind went blank', 'super nervous', and 'anxiety'. That's fear, plain and simple. They have been rejected so many times they feel awful about themselves. And underneath all of it is something very real: they need a job to pay their bills.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming exactly what hurts: rejected again and again, then freezing up when it counts most. Tell them straight that their qualifications aren't the problem. Then show them there is a fix.
prose_plain.implication: They've read the generic tips, redone their CV until a professional approved it, and sent it out over 200 times. Nothing changed. They're not looking for more advice about formatting or eye contact, because they've had all of that and still get rejected. What they need is a real explanation for why it keeps happening, one that actually fits their specific situation.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop being rejected and stop going blank in interviews so they can finally get a job that matches what they are actually capable of.
prose_plain.push: They've been rejected over 30 times and they completely froze in an interview, mind went blank, and they still don't know why it keeps happening.
prose_plain.pull: They want more interviews to actually come through, and when they get one, they want to get through it without anxiety taking over.
prose_plain.anxiety: They keep asking themselves what they're doing wrong, even though their CV has been checked and approved. They're scared the next interview will go exactly like the last one, blank mind and all.
prose_plain.habit: They keep sending out more CVs and rereading their resume, repeating the same things that haven't worked, because they don't have anything else to try.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: After 30-plus rejections they don't trust their own judgement anymore, so they need to see that someone credible has diagnosed this kind of problem before and solved it. They're also watching for people who've been in the same streak and got out, because that's the only proof they'll believe right now. And because their confidence is shot, they won't act on vague guidance, they need a clear, repeatable practice they can follow step by step so they feel less like they're winging it.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Parents are calling this an addiction. One parent said they wanted to 'reverse the effect of excessive screen time on my 19-month-old.' That isn't mild worry. That's a parent who is scared their child is already damaged. The feeling driving them is protective love, and right now it is mixed with fear.
prose_plain.lead_with: They have already decided screens are a problem. What they want now is a real method. Show them a step-by-step way to wean the child off and swap screens for something else. Then tell them straight that the damage isn't permanent. That reassurance counts as much as the plan.
prose_plain.implication: They've already read the articles about screen time limits and downloaded the parental control apps. That advice is everywhere and it hasn't fixed anything, so they don't trust a version of it they haven't heard before. What they're looking for feels different from 'set a timer and hold firm,' because they've held firm and the screaming got louder.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Wean my child off screen dependence and undo its effects without constant battles
prose_plain.push: Their child seems addicted to screens and they're scared the harm is already happening at an age when it shouldn't be reversible.
prose_plain.pull: They want a way to wean their child off screens and undo what's happened, without a daily battle they don't have the energy to win.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid the damage is already permanent, and they're also afraid that taking the screen away just makes the meltdowns worse than the screen itself.
prose_plain.habit: They hand over the device because it's the only thing that buys them five quiet minutes, and in that moment the quiet wins.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're scared they've already caused harm to a developing brain, so they defer fast to anyone who sounds like a child development expert rather than a parenting blogger. They also need to see other parents who had the same addicted-toddler fear and came out the other side, because without that they assume their situation is too far gone. And they feel the clock running, believing a 19-month-old's brain is in a window that's closing, which means they move quickly when something feels credible.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These buyers are scared of being rejected by the people they love most. They want to come out, but they are terrified of disappointing their parents or losing the people who count to them. Some are so stressed they feel lost in the moment. The core need is simple: be accepted as they are, and keep those close relationships safe.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they want to come out. They don't need convincing. What they need is a clear, step-by-step path that shows them how to do it without everything falling apart. Start there.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to 'just be themselves' so many times it's stopped meaning anything. The advice was never wrong, but it never told them what to actually say, how to pace it, or how to stay safe while doing it. They're not looking for a nudge anymore, they're looking for something concrete that accounts for real consequences.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Tell the people who count who I really am, and not lose their love or my safety in the process.
prose_plain.push: They're having panic attacks and carrying chronic stress because they're still hiding who they are every single day.
prose_plain.pull: They want the relief of being fully known and still loved, without the weight of keeping the secret anymore.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're convinced the people they love will be disappointed, pull away, or that being honest will put them in an unsafe situation.
prose_plain.habit: They keep presenting as straight because they've spent years reassuring people, and staying hidden still feels like the less dangerous option.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel less alone when they can see that other people who looked exactly like them, closeted, scared, sure it would go badly, came out and kept their relationships intact. They trust someone who's guided people through this before because the stakes feel too high to figure it out alone. Belonging to a group of people who've already walked this path makes the whole thing feel survivable instead of theoretical.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: People want to learn properly and fast. They want to communicate well. But the real fear is freezing up mid-conversation and looking foolish in front of others. Being fluent, being someone who speaks multiple languages, that feels like something worth becoming.
prose_plain.lead_with: Your buyers have already studied. They just can't speak when it counts. Lead with that. Show them a way to fix the output problem. Skip the pitch about why learning a language counts. They already know.
prose_plain.implication: They've already bought apps, courses, and YouTube playlists that promised fluency. Every one of those things taught them more words they still can't say out loud when someone's standing in front of them. They don't distrust effort, they distrust the idea that more studying will fix what studying already didn't fix.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Speak the language in a real conversation. Not just study it.
prose_plain.push: They've put in real time studying and they still freeze the second a real conversation starts, and that gap kills their motivation.
prose_plain.pull: They want to be in a real conversation, speaking without panic, feeling like someone who actually knows the language.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're worried they'll get distracted and quit again, or that they still won't have the right guides to learn it the way it's supposed to be done.
prose_plain.habit: They keep going back to passive studying, or they stop altogether, because both feel safer than the risk of opening their mouth and getting it wrong.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust someone who's visibly fluent, or better yet, multilingual, because that person is proof it's possible and not just theory. They're moved by stories from people who were just as stuck as they are now and then started speaking, because that matches exactly where they're sitting. Small daily speaking commitments work on them because they've already quit once, and a low-stakes promise they can keep feels safer than a big goal they've already broken.

prose_plain.lead_with: Start by naming the feeling they already have: stuck in the middle, their manager expects results, their team won't listen, and nobody seems to respect them. Show them there's a clear way through that. Do that before you mention any tools or methods.
prose_plain.implication: They've already seen the listicles and the '5 steps to better leadership' content, and none of it made the team respect them any more than before. They've been promised that the right model or the right phrase will fix things, and it hasn't. So they're not looking for another tidy system, they're looking for proof that someone actually understands how hard and lonely this specific moment feels.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop being the person who does the work and start being the person who leads the team. Earn the team's respect while doing it.
prose_plain.push: They got promoted with no training, their team won't take direction from them, and every time they try to hand off work they freeze up because it feels like something will go wrong.
prose_plain.pull: They want the team to run well without them holding every thread, and they want to actually like being around the people they manage.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid they'll get it badly wrong in front of everyone and the team will see they were never cut out for this role.
prose_plain.habit: When things get hard they go back to heads-down individual work, doing tasks themselves instead of leading, because that's what always felt safe before the promotion.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They got promoted with no guidance, so they're actively looking for someone credible to tell them what good looks like, because no one at work is doing that. They also feel like they're the only one struggling this badly, so hearing that most new managers get no training at all makes them breathe again. And when they find a coach who speaks directly to the first-time manager experience, they feel like they've found their people rather than a generic self-help audience.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: A lot of people in this market are scared they will die young, just like a parent did. That fear is personal. It isn't abstract. It ties straight to wanting to be there for their own kids.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start with the fear of following a parent to an early grave, and the wish to stay alive for family. Bring in any programme or approach after that.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen every 'live longer' headline, bought the supplements, read the articles, and none of it spoke to their specific fear: that their family history is a sentence they can't appeal. The broad promises feel like noise now because nothing has ever addressed what they're actually scared of. They're not cynical about health in general, they're cynical about anything that doesn't reckon with what happened to their parent.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to improve their odds of a long, healthy life, avoid dying young the way their family did, and still be around for their kids.
prose_plain.push: They lost a parent early and now they're scared the same thing is coming for them.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel like their choices actually shape how long and how well they live.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that if it's genetic, all the effort in the world won't save them.

prose_plain.lead_with: The sharpest pain here is feeling like a failure and believing they've missed their chance. Start there. Show them it isn't too late at 40 or 50, and back it up with real examples of people who started over late and made it work.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen plenty of 'reinvent yourself' content before and it didn't stick, because it never spoke to being 50 with nothing rebuilt yet. The advice always felt written for someone younger, or someone who still had options. prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me believe I still have time, then show me exactly how to rebuild a life I can be proud of after 40 or 50.
prose_plain.push: They feel like their life has added up to failure. They've lost a job, or a relationship, or both, and the money isn't there either. The spark they used to feel is just gone.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel genuinely excited about their life again, the kind of excitement they haven't felt in years. They want to look at where they are and actually feel proud of it, not just relieved.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that the effort won't pay off because too much time has already passed. They worry that starting over at this age means they'll run out of runway before anything real gets built.
prose_plain.habit: They keep looking at what other people their age have achieved and use it as evidence that they've fallen behind for good. That comparison pulls them straight back into the story that they've failed, and they stay stuck there.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't believe reassurance from someone who hasn't stood where they're standing, so they need to see real people who restarted from a low point at the same age and came out the other side. A clear roadmap does something specific for them: it makes the whole thing feel less like a wish and more like a thing that can actually happen in steps. And they won't trust a coach who feels polished or far removed from struggle, because that distance makes them feel like an edge case instead of someone who can be helped.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: The deepest pain here isn't fear. It's loss. Loss of belonging, loss of structure, loss of the people. 'I was useless to society.' 'I was alone.' The chow hall. The 40-man barracks. The buddies. That's what they are grieving. Not danger. Not excitement. The people and the routine that made life feel like it made sense.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know transition is hard. They're living it. What they don't know is why it hurts this much. Start there. Name the loss of identity, the loss of the tribe, the loss of the structure that told them who they were. Tell them that is the real reason it is so hard. Make them feel understood before you offer anything.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen the generic reintegration advice, the checklists, the 'thank you for your service' content that names the problem without actually knowing it. None of it talked about losing the chow hall, the 40-man barracks, the automatic sense of who they were when they woke up. So they stopped believing the people giving advice had ever really felt what they're feeling.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me figure out who I am and where I belong now that the military's structure and my brothers are gone.
prose_plain.push: They feel useless and alone, and the shock of how different civilian life is hasn't worn off the way they thought it would.
prose_plain.pull: They want to understand why this transition is so hard and find a way through it that's actually worked for people like them.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that struggling this much, especially if they were never in combat, means something is fundamentally wrong with them.
prose_plain.habit: They go quiet, pull away from people, and try to white-knuckle the whole thing on their own without telling anyone how bad it is.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They came from a world built entirely on brotherhood, and they're desperately looking for that in-group feeling again, so they buy from someone who's clearly one of them, not just someone who studied them. They don't trust easily, but when they see other vets who struggled the same way and came out the other side, the shame loosens a little and they start to think it might actually be possible for them too.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Men in this market talk about wanting to 'be the man I want to be' and 'become a better man.' The 'man up' jokes show they fear being laughed at when they struggle. The 'can't satisfy my wife' comment tells you this is also about their relationship. They want to measure up. They're scared of what people will think if they don't.
prose_plain.lead_with: These men feel like they are failing or going numb, but they have no word for it and no idea what to do next. Start by naming what they feel ('you're not broken, you were never taught this'). Do that before you show them what to do. Name the pain first. Path second.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen a thousand 'be a better man' ads, posts, and programs, and every one of them made the same vague promise without showing them how to actually hold a job, stay connected, and feel okay in their own skin at the same time. They've tried pushing through on their own, and they've tried being told to 'open up', and neither one worked. So they don't trust the promise anymore unless something shows them it's different in a way they can feel, not just read.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Become a man I actually respect. Someone who is steady, capable, and can open up without being made to feel small for it.
prose_plain.push: They feel like a failure who can't hold things together at work or connect with the people they love, and when they try to say so, they get told to man up, which makes them feel even more alone.
prose_plain.pull: They want a clear, real way to be strong and emotionally open at the same time, and to be respected for it, not mocked.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that if they let their guard down, it'll blow up in their face and people will see them as weak.
prose_plain.habit: They stay quiet and stoic because that's always been the safe move, and they don't know what breaks them out of it without costing them something.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't follow just anyone because they've been burned by advice that didn't come from someone who actually lived this, so they need to see that a real man they respect has already walked this road. Seeing other men do the work and come out more respected, not less, is what makes it feel safe enough to try, because right now their whole fear is that they'll be the only one who looks weak. And when the work is wrapped in a brotherhood, it stops being a therapy thing and starts being something men do together, which fits who they already want to be.

prose_plain.t4_name: They're sure vulnerability will cost them

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These buyers are in real pain. You see it in what they say: 'I feel hollow and empty and purposeless', 'I still hate myself', 'now I feel ugly and worthless'. That isn't frustration. That's someone whose sense of self has been gutted. Alongside that, they are desperate to feel liked and valued again. They keep craving the ex's approval. They ask how to get their self-esteem back. Two wounds, not one: the emptiness inside, and the need to feel worth something to other people.
prose_plain.lead_with: Name the exact pain before you offer anything. Say it out loud: you went no contact and you still miss him, and you hate yourself for missing him. They already know it hurts. What they don't know is why it still hurts when they are doing what everyone told them to do. Start there. Name the specific agony first. Then you can talk about what helps.
prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'just go no contact' and they did it, and the obsessive thoughts didn't stop. They've been told time heals this, but months later they're still checking the ex's social media and blaming themselves. The standard recovery advice feels like it was written for a different kind of breakup, not what happened to them.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop obsessing over the ex, get their self-worth back, and feel like themselves again.
prose_plain.push: They're doing no contact and it's not helping. The pain is just as loud weeks or months in, and that scares them because they thought this was the fix.
prose_plain.pull: They want a way to actually get the ex out of their head and feel like a real person again, someone with worth who doesn't need that approval anymore.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they'll cave around the three-week mark like they always do, and even more scared that nothing will ever actually work for them specifically.
prose_plain.habit: They ruminate, they check on the ex, they run the same self-blame loops over and over, and even though it hurts, it feels like the only way they still have any connection to what happened.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need a coach who can name exactly what's happening inside them, because when someone explains the 'why' precisely, it's the first time they've felt sane in months and that builds instant trust. They're also starving for proof that someone like them actually got better, not just coped, because they've stopped believing general success stories and only trust voices from people who were also discarded. They feel a deep pull toward others who share that specific identity, because being understood by their own kind is the first real relief they've felt.

prose_plain.t2_name: No contact stopped working for them

prose_plain.t4_name: They think they'll always cave

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Money is on the line: a salary left on the table, a price they should have pushed back on, a job offer they just accepted. But underneath that is something that hurts more. They feel like people walk all over them. They know they're too nice. They hate direct disagreement, so they say yes when they mean no, and they feel bad about it afterwards.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start with the self-blame. They caved. They let it happen again. They know it. Lead with that feeling, then show them they can hold their ground without the confrontation they dread.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen the BATNA explainers and the hardball tactics and none of it felt like something they could actually do without their hands shaking. The advice they've gotten assumes they're comfortable with tension, and they're not. So they've filed it away as 'works for other people' and kept accepting the first number they're handed.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop giving in and get what they're worth, without the uncomfortable confrontation they hate
prose_plain.push: They caved on salary or price, someone walked over them, and now they're replaying it and wishing they'd said something different.
prose_plain.pull: They want to ask for more and actually get it, without turning the conversation into a confrontation they dread for days beforehand.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that pushing back means the other person gets angry, thinks badly of them, or walks away entirely.
prose_plain.habit: They accept the first offer, they stay quiet when something feels wrong, and they tell themselves they're just being nice.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're not going to trust their gut in a high-stakes moment because their gut has told them to cave every time before, so they need a method that feels airtight and comes from someone who clearly knows what they're doing. They also need to have already decided what they won't accept before the conversation starts, because in the moment their instinct is to fold. And when the approach feels calm and likable rather than combative, it stops feeling like something that'll blow up the relationship, which is the fear that's been stopping them.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: The pain here is raw. People say things like "it's torture, I just cry" and "I can't stand it anymore." That's not frustration. That's someone at breaking point. On top of that, they're terrified the thoughts mean something about who they are as a person. Thoughts about harming others, or being a predator, or being evil. They're not just scared of the thoughts. They're scared the thoughts prove they're a monster.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they have OCD. They've Googled it. They don't need you to explain what intrusive thoughts are. What they need is to believe there's a real way out. Start by showing them why everything they've tried hasn't worked, and that there's a specific approach that does. Give them a reason to trust the solution before you sell anything.
prose_plain.implication: They've already been told to think positive, distract themselves, or just let the thoughts pass. They tried it and the thoughts came back louder, so they now believe the standard advice doesn't work for what they have. They don't think they're hard to help because they're resistant; they think they're hard to help because what they have is uniquely shameful and uniquely stubborn.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want the thoughts gone for good, not just managed. And they want to know, without any doubt, that having the thoughts doesn't make them a bad person.
prose_plain.push: They're in what they call torture. They cry, they can't stand it, and it's bleeding into their studies and their daily life until they feel like they can't function.
prose_plain.pull: They want the thoughts genuinely gone, not managed or quieted for a while but stopped for good so they never have to white-knuckle through a day like this again.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that wanting help means the thoughts are true, and that a professional will confirm they really are dangerous or evil rather than sick.
prose_plain.habit: They keep seeking reassurance that they're not bad, and they keep trying to push the thoughts out of their head, and both things feed the loop and make it worse.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't trust someone who speaks in general wellness terms, because they've heard that and it didn't touch what they're going through. They need to see that someone with real clinical weight has worked specifically with people who had the same horrifying thoughts and came out the other side, because that's the only thing that starts to loosen the shame. When they hear that others had thoughts exactly like theirs and weren't monsters, it cracks open the belief that they're uniquely evil in a way nothing else does.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Parents say things like 'give my child the best' and 'parent them to become better than me.' That's love talking. But they also say 'feel like a failure,' 'don't want to be that parent,' and 'mom guilt.' That's about who they are, not just what they do. Both count.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they want to stop yelling. Don't tell them that's the goal. Start by explaining why the quick tips they've already tried didn't work, and what's actually keeping the cycle going.
prose_plain.implication: They've read the lists, watched the reels, downloaded the guides. They know what they're supposed to do and they still lose it at their kids, which makes them feel worse than if they'd never learned any of it. They've been told it's about behaviour and scripts, so when those don't stick, they assume the problem is them.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop yelling and losing my temper so I don't pass on the damage my parents did to me, and so my child gets something better.
prose_plain.push: They're yelling at their kids and then feeling wrecked with guilt, and that loop keeps repeating however hard they try to stop it.
prose_plain.pull: They want to actually show up calm and present, give their kids something better than what they had, and feel like a good mom while they're doing it.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that even if they get better for a while, the damage is already done, or they'll slide back into exactly what their own parents did.
prose_plain.habit: They lose their temper, feel awful about it, apologise to their kid, promise themselves it won't happen again, and then it does.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're already drowning in shame, so they shut down the second they feel judged, which means they'll only stay with a coach who feels warm and genuinely on their side. Seeing other moms in the same cycle tells them they're not broken or uniquely terrible, and that relief is what gets them to keep reading. A coach who clearly knows the deeper stuff about regulation, not just behaviour tricks, earns their trust because it matches what they've privately suspected all along.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These parents love their kid and want to stay connected to her. But they also need to feel like they did a good job raising her. When someone says 'my other three children do fine,' they're not bragging. They're defending themselves. They want proof the problem isn't them.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start with the thing they actually want: a teen who talks to them and treats them with respect. Then show them there's a calmer way to get there. They already know shouting and punishing isn't working. They just don't know what to do instead.
prose_plain.implication: They've already heard 'set firm boundaries' and 'be consistent' and they were consistent and it didn't work. Punishment felt like doing something, so they did more of it, and the distance just got wider. They don't need another generic fix, they need someone to explain why their daughter is acting this way so the approach actually makes sense to them.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get back to a relationship where their teen respects them and talks to them, without turning every conversation into a fight or giving up their authority as a parent.
prose_plain.push: Their daughter was fine, and then over the past year she wasn't, and nothing they've tried has brought her back.
prose_plain.pull: They want a real conversation with her again, one where she actually opens up instead of shutting down.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that trying one more thing is just more proof they've been doing it wrong all along.
prose_plain.habit: They keep reaching for punishment because it feels like action, even though they already know it's not working.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're carrying quiet shame that they broke something in their kid, so they need an expert to tell them plainly that this isn't what bad parenting looks like. They also need to hear that other good, trying parents have been in this exact spot and came out the other side, because that's the only thing that makes hope feel real. And they won't hear any of it from someone who makes them feel judged, even slightly, because they're already saying that to themselves every day.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: They say things like 'I can't say no' and 'socialising wipes me out'. That's the pain talking. They also say they're scared of burning out again or ending up in the same kind of draining relationship. That's fear talking. Both are real and both drive them to look for help.
prose_plain.lead_with: These people already know what they are. They call themselves people-pleasers. They call it codependency. So don't explain the problem back to them. Lead with a way out of it, one that goes to the root, not just the surface habit.
prose_plain.implication: They've read the books, they know the word codependency, and they've probably tried to set a boundary or two. But the advice they've gotten has lived on the surface, telling them to just say no, as if the habit isn't wired into them from childhood. They've been promised that awareness is enough, and it wasn't, so they're skeptical that anything goes deep enough to actually change the pattern.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to stop giving everything away and saying yes to things they hate, so they can actually have relationships without running on empty or disappearing into someone else.
prose_plain.push: They're burnt out and drained from constantly giving to everyone around them, and socializing feels like a performance they're exhausted by before it even starts.
prose_plain.pull: They want to learn how to say no, understand why they keep ending up in the same patterns, and finally stop handing themselves over to relationships that leave them empty.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if they stop people-pleasing, the people they love will leave, and they're scared they'll end up in another codependent relationship even if they do the work.
prose_plain.habit: Saying yes is automatic for them, it started in childhood and it doesn't feel like a choice, it feels like who they are.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel less alone when they're in a room, even a virtual one, with people who also grew up as the accommodating one, because it stops feeling like a personal flaw and starts feeling like something that happened to them. They trust someone who can explain why their nervous system does this, not just that it does, because that explanation is the first thing that's ever made them feel like change is actually possible. And when they make one small commitment, like saying no once and surviving it, their brain starts to rewrite the story they've told themselves about who they are.

prose_plain.lead_with: These buyers already know perfectionism is their problem. They aren't looking to be diagnosed. Start with what they actually want: a way to do good work without freezing up or beating themselves up every time something falls short.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to just lower the bar, embrace imperfection, and ship it. That advice felt like a threat, not a solution, because their standards are part of how they see themselves as capable and credible. They're not looking to stop caring, they're looking for a way to care and still move.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me get things done and finished without the paralysis or the constant self-criticism when the result isn't perfect.
prose_plain.push: They're stuck, missing deadlines, and burning out because their own standards have become a trap they can't get out of.
prose_plain.pull: They want to act, finish things, and ship work without the constant grinding feeling that it's still not good enough.

They respond to other high achievers who let go and still came out respected, because that's the only proof that counts to them. And they're more likely to change when they make small commitments first, because their whole identity is built on following through.

prose_plain.lead_with: They've already picked real estate. So don't sell them on why real estate. Speak to the two things stopping them: fear, and not having much money to start with.
prose_plain.implication: They've been saturated with promises of passive income and financial freedom from coaches selling the dream louder than they explain the path. They've seen enough no-money-down pitches that the phrase itself makes them suspicious now. What they haven't seen is someone who shows them exactly how one real deal worked and what happened when it got hard.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Do their first deal and start building passive income, even with little money and a lot of fear.
prose_plain.push: Real estate feels impossibly complicated to them, and they've been sitting in research mode so long that it's starting to feel like the research is the job.
prose_plain.pull: They want income that shows up without them trading hours for it, and they want a way in that doesn't require a pile of money they don't have.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid of losing money, and they've watched enough people get burned that the fear feels completely reasonable to them.
prose_plain.habit: When doubt creeps in, they go find more information instead of taking a step, and that loop has kept them from doing a first deal for longer than they'd like to admit.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're beginners, so they don't trust their own judgement yet, and they default to whoever looks like they've done this for real and can prove it. Peer stories hit hard because they're not asking if it's possible in theory, they're asking if someone like them actually pulled it off. And because they're frozen in research mode, a deal or opportunity framed as time-limited gives them the external pressure their own motivation can't supply.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Some people in this market have no food, no money, and no way to pay their bills. Some are back living with their parents. That's basic survival. On top of that, many feel like a failure or worthless. That's about who they think they are, not just what they have in the bank.
prose_plain.lead_with: These people are in pain and panic at the same time. Start by telling them this is grief, not a character flaw. Then give them one concrete thing to do right now. They need both. Either one without the other won't hold their attention.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen the generic 'update your CV and network' advice everywhere, and it didn't change anything for them. They already worked hard and still ended up here, so the standard job-search promises feel hollow now. What they haven't been offered is someone who speaks to the identity collapse, not just the empty bank account.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get back on my feet. Rebuild my income and my sense of self after losing my job.
prose_plain.push: They've lost the job and with it their sense of worth, and the financial pressure is immediate and real, bills, rent, sometimes basic food, and the guilt and devastation sit on top of all of it.
prose_plain.pull: They want to be earning again, but more than that they want to feel like a capable, worthwhile person, not someone who failed.
prose_plain.anxiety: They already tried hard and it didn't protect them, so they're scared that if they put themselves out there again and it still doesn't work, that proves once and for all that they're not good enough.
prose_plain.habit: They pull inward, sit in the shame, and start telling themselves they've given up, because the job felt like part of who they are and losing it feels like losing themselves.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're ashamed, and shame makes people feel alone in their situation, so hearing that real people came back from exactly this is what cracks the door open. They're also in crisis, which means they're scared of making another wrong move, so a coach who clearly knows this territory makes them feel safer. And because shame shuts people down, they won't open up to someone who feels cold or clinical, they buy from someone who feels like they understand what it actually feels like.

They say things like 'I feel like I'm disappearing' and 'I no longer have friends.' What they actually want, underneath all of it, is to feel connected and to have a real life with real people around them. That's the need this market isn't getting met.
prose_plain.lead_with: Name the loneliness exactly as it feels before you mention any fix. Say it out loud before you talk about community, coliving, or building a routine.
prose_plain.implication: They've been sold 'work from anywhere' and 'total freedom' so many times that those words don't do anything for them anymore. They chose this life for the promise, and the promise delivered on logistics but left them eating dinner alone and watching group chats they're not in. They're not looking for more freedom. They already have it and they're lonely inside it.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Keep my remote life and my freedom, but stop feeling invisible and alone while I live it.
prose_plain.push: They feel like they're fading. Friends back home moved on, coworkers don't exist, and the freedom they worked hard for has started to feel like being cut off from everyone.
prose_plain.pull: They want a setup where connection is already built in, coliving spaces, coworking programs, people they didn't have to hunt down on their own.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that fixing the loneliness means giving up the lifestyle, or that any 'community' they join will feel hollow and performative.
prose_plain.habit: They stay home, they stay online, and they keep telling themselves the tradeoff is worth it even when it's clearly not.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Because belonging is what they're actually starving for, seeing people like them who found real connection without giving up the lifestyle is the one thing that feels true. They're wary of anything that feels like a forced networking event dressed up as community, so warmth and realness from people who get it are what get past their guard. They don't need to be convinced the problem is real. They need to see that other people like them solved it.

prose_plain.lead_with: They already know the destination. They know saving more is part of the answer. What they need is a way to get there from where they actually are right now, including if they are starting late or starting over.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen the FIRE content, they know what a savings rate is, and they've probably made a budget more than once. prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get to a safe retirement or early financial independence without the fear of running out of money, even if they feel behind.
prose_plain.push: They're afraid. Some of them have virtually no savings and no clear path to retirement, and the fear that they may never get to stop working sits with them every day.
prose_plain.pull: They want to reach financial independence in a defined number of years, or at least retire comfortably without spending their last decade in dread.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that past false starts and poor financial choices have already decided their future, and that starting over at this point won't be enough.
prose_plain.habit: They avoid looking at the numbers directly. The question 'how do I save money again' shows they've tried before, lost the thread, and haven't fully committed to a system that holds.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Because the stakes are their entire financial future, they won't trust someone who just sounds good. They need to see badges or a track record they can verify before they'll listen at all. They also scan hard for people who were in the same position they're in now, because that's the only proof that feels real to them.

prose_plain.lead_with: Start with the pain of losing deals and giving away margin through discounts. Then hit the fear of rejection. Then promise they can close with confidence without ever feeling like they are pushing someone.
prose_plain.implication: They've seen every closing technique in the book. prose_plain.jtbd_job: Confidently close more deals without feeling pushy or relying on discounts
prose_plain.push: They're losing deals they should win, their margins are shrinking every time they cave and cut the price, and the rejection is starting to feel personal enough that they dread picking up the phone.
prose_plain.pull: They want to get to yes without pushing, without apologising, and without shaving money off the deal just to make the discomfort stop. They want to hit their number and feel okay about how they got there.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're worried that any new approach will just turn them into a slicker version of the pushy salesperson they already hate, or that they'll try it and still get rejected and still cave.
prose_plain.habit: They keep dropping the price the moment a prospect hesitates, and they've mostly stopped doing cold outreach because the silence or the no feels worse than just working the warm leads they already have.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't trust a coaching promise from someone who hasn't clearly lived inside a sales room and won there, so authority from real experience is what gets them to listen at all. Once they're listening, they need to see people who look like them hitting quota without discounting, because that's the only proof that it's possible for someone in their shoes. And they're already wired to follow a process step by step, so when a method asks them to commit to small actions and build on each one, it fits how they already think about getting better.

prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that wanting a break makes them a bad parent, and they're scared someone will judge them or wave their pain away again.

prose_plain.lead_with: Start with the pain they know by name: burnout, the shame after a startup fails, the quiet fear that they were never cut out for this. Earn their attention there before you say a word about your approach.
prose_plain.implication: They've absorbed years of 'just push harder' content and 'success is one habit away' promises, and those promises are part of why they burned out. They've tried grinding through it and they've tried stepping back, and neither one brought them back to themselves. At this point, a bare promise of founder success reads as more of the same noise that broke them.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to feel like a capable founder again and get their momentum back, without wrecking their health to do it.
prose_plain.push: Their startup failed or is falling apart, and the burnout hit so hard they feel empty, useless, and like they've lost any discipline they ever had.
prose_plain.pull: They want to find their purpose again, stop running on empty, and build something that actually pays, without sacrificing who they are to do it.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that they're not cut out for this, that they'll burn out again the moment they try, and that the failure already proved something true and damning about them.
prose_plain.habit: When it gets hard, they either crawl back toward a corporate job for safety or they put their head down and grind through the pain because they believe suffering is what being a real founder costs.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust advice from people who've only won, because winning advice is what got them into this mess. They need to see that someone who's shipped and failed is still standing and still building, because that's the only proof that recovery is real. And they're deeply isolated right now, so the feeling that there's a room of people who've been exactly here, people who get it without explanation, is what makes them lean in.

prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they are overpaying. You don't need to convince them of the problem. Lead with the specific thing that fixes it. Show them how self-employed people legally cut their tax bill. The more specific the better.

prose_plain.push: They're paying more in taxes as a self-employed person than they did as a W-2 employee, sometimes while earning the same or less, and that feels like a penalty for working for themselves.
prose_plain.pull: They want a legal way to bring their self-employment tax bill down and stop feeling like they're overpaying every single year.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're worried they'll file wrong, miss something they were supposed to claim, or worse, trigger an audit, and some of them aren't even sure whether they owe what they've been told they owe.
prose_plain.habit: They file the basic way every year and assume the high bill is just the cost of being self-employed, so they never look for a smarter approach.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're handing over their financial and legal exposure to a stranger, so badges aren't a nice touch, they're the price of entry. And because tax savings are tied to deadlines they can't move, a closing window feels genuinely real to them, not manufactured.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These people are in real pain right now. Vivid flashbacks, moments where reality slips away, searching for something that gives relief fast. This isn't abstract suffering. They want to feel safer today.
prose_plain.lead_with: Start by saying out loud what they live with. The flashbacks. The people who told them to shut up about it. Let them feel heard first. Then, and only then, show them that recovery is real.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to breathe through it, journal it out, or just give it time. None of that stopped a flashback when it hit, so they've stopped trusting advice that sounds general and calm. They're looking for something specific enough to use in the moment, from someone who clearly knows what C-PTSD actually does to a person.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get relief from flashbacks right now, and find proof that recovery from C-PTSD is actually possible for someone like them.
prose_plain.push: They're having vivid flashbacks that pull them out of the present, and the people closest to them tell them they're overreacting or making it up.
prose_plain.pull: They want something they can do right now when a flashback hits, and they want real evidence that people with C-PTSD actually recover fully.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that their trauma is too complex or too severe to recover from, and that they're looking at a lifetime of just managing it.
prose_plain.habit: They've been getting through it alone, without anyone who believes them and without a tool that actually works when things go bad.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've been dismissed by family and sometimes by clinicians, so they don't trust just anyone who calls themselves a coach. A coach who speaks their clinical language and has lived experience of recovery answers the question they're actually asking, which is whether someone like them can get better. Hearing from others who recovered from the same severity of trauma is the only thing that makes that feel real rather than theoretical.

prose_plain.t2_name: They slipped out of reality again
prose_plain.t3_name: They want proof recovery is real
prose_plain.t4_name: They think complex trauma is permanent

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These women say things like 'I'm a people pleaser and I'm tired of it,' 'I'm afraid to speak up,' 'I feel bad when I do,' and 'it keeps landing me in bad situations.' They feel fear and guilt around keeping others happy. What they want is to feel confident and powerful and to finally stand up for themselves.
prose_plain.lead_with: They feel used and burnt out, but they blame themselves for it. Start by telling them people-pleasing is something they learned, not something they are. That shift counts before anything else.
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to 'be more confident' and 'love yourself' so many times that the words have stopped meaning anything. They've tried affirmations and pep talks and still said yes when they wanted to say no, so they're not looking for another mindset speech. What they're listening for now is something that explains why they keep doing this even when they hate it, and shows them a way out that feels real.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop abandoning myself. Learn to say no, set boundaries, and feel good about it instead of guilty.
prose_plain.push: They're burned out and resentful from saying yes over and over, and they know they're doing it to themselves, which makes it worse.
prose_plain.pull: They want to be the kind of woman who respects herself enough to say no and doesn't spiral into guilt afterward.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that putting themselves first makes them a bad person, selfish, or someone other people will stop loving.
prose_plain.habit: Even when they see what's happening, the guilt and the lifelong pull to keep everyone happy drags them back to yes every time.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust one person telling them it's possible, but when they see women who looked exactly like them, stuck in the same pattern, who actually got out of it, something shifts. They're also carrying a lot of shame about who they've been, so they won't open up to someone who feels polished or distant. They buy from someone who sounds like she's sat in the same seat and doesn't make them feel small for being there.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: These people are in real physical pain. They use words like 'serious, serious burnout', 'I still feel exhausted', 'no amount of rest will help'. Their body is running on empty and they know it. What they want most is to stop feeling this way and to function like a normal human being again.
prose_plain.lead_with: They already know they are burned out. They have also tried resting and it didn't fix anything. Start there. Tell them why rest alone didn't work, and what actually getting better looks like.
prose_plain.implication: They've already tried the obvious things. Sleep, weekends off, holidays, cutting back on coffee, all of it, and none of it touched the exhaustion underneath. So when they hear 'rest more' or 'practice self-care,' they don't just ignore it, they actively distrust whoever's saying it, because they've already been down that road and it didn't go anywhere.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get my energy back and feel like myself again, without having to walk away from my job.
prose_plain.push: They worked hard for too long and now no amount of rest makes a dent, and that frightens them.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know how someone actually healed from serious burnout, and how long it honestly took.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that nothing will work because rest already failed them, and they can't quit the job that's draining them.
prose_plain.habit: They keep pushing through the same job, resting passively on weekends, and waiting to feel better on their own.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're not looking for theory, they're looking for someone who's actually seen this get better, because their own experience has given them real reasons to doubt that it can. Hearing from people who came back from the same kind of exhaustion is the only thing that makes hope feel reasonable rather than naive. And because they're depleted and wary, they won't warm up to someone who sounds clinical or preachy, they need to feel like the person talking to them actually gets it.

prose_plain.lf8_evidence: Writers here are scared people will judge their work and find it bad. They worry they have no right to write at all. But underneath that fear is a real hunger: they want to prove, to themselves more than anyone, that they can finish a book and put it into the world. That counts with them deeply.
prose_plain.lead_with: These writers already know they should push through. They don't need convincing that writing is worth doing. What they need is a clear process that gets the draft finished even on the days when doubt is loud. Lead with that.
prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'just keep writing' and 'show up every day' so many times it sounds like noise now. Every productivity tip, writing challenge, and word-count tracker promised momentum and delivered a few good days before the stall came back. They're not looking for more advice about writing, they're looking for proof that someone like them actually got to the end.
prose_plain.jtbd_job: Actually finish the book I started, instead of stalling at chapter one.
prose_plain.push: They're stuck in the middle of a project they care about, and the self-doubt has gotten loud enough to stop them from opening the file.
prose_plain.pull: They want consistent forward movement and a finished manuscript they can feel good about.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that finishing the book will just prove the voice in their head right, that nobody will read it and they were never a real writer.
prose_plain.habit: They wait until they feel ready or inspired, and because that feeling rarely shows up on schedule, weeks go by without words on the page.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust themselves as a source of authority right now, so they borrow it from someone who has a finished book to their name. A coach who's published signals that finishing is real and learnable, not just luck. And when they see other stuck writers who crossed the finish line, it chips away at the story they've been telling themselves that they're the one person this won't work for.

prose_plain.implication: They've been handed planners, apps, and early-morning routines their whole lives, and none of it stuck. prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've spent most of their life feeling like they're failing at rules built for someone else's brain, so when someone speaks their experience back to them exactly, they feel found rather than fixed. Clinical authority does something specific for them: it swaps shame for explanation, which makes trying one more time feel less like a risk. And when they hear someone else say getting diagnosed changed everything, that's the closest thing to proof they've ever had that this could work for them too.
prose_plain.push: They can't follow through on tasks at work, they lose track of time constantly, and their boss has already said something about it out loud.

prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that a diagnosis won't change anything because the real problem is that they're just lazy. They feel like taking medication makes them look like an addict. And they can't easily afford a doctor to even find out.
prose_plain.habit: They skip medication because it feels complicated or shameful. They stay in bed when the day already feels too big. They avoid the tasks that feel impossible to start.

prose_plain.implication: They've been told 'you can do this' and 'just take it one day at a time' so many times that the words don't do anything for them anymore.
