prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're standing in a place that feels uniquely shameful, so hearing from someone who stood in the exact same spot and didn't stay broken is the only thing that actually cuts through. When they say out loud 'I'm new here' or 'I'm trying again,' that small public step is hard to walk back from, and it keeps them showing up. They don't want to be lectured at by someone who never lived it, they want to be seen by people who did.
prose_plain.push: Their drinking has hurt people they love, brought them close to losing everything, and put them within reach of consequences they can't undo.
prose_plain.pull: They believe sobriety opens a better life, and they hold onto other people's encouragement and the idea that there are real things to feel and do instead of drinking.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they'll lose their social life completely, that loneliness and depression are just what sober feels like, and that stopping drinking means losing a version of themselves they can't get back.
prose_plain.habit: They've leaned on alcohol to feel comfortable around other people for so long that stopping feels like showing up to every situation without any armour, and the first few days go fine until something social or stressful breaks the streak.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Understand and push back on how adoption works and who it serves
prose_plain.note: This buyer thinks critically about adoption as a system. They aren't primarily processing personal pain. They want to question, research, and advocate for change.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to feel like they belong
prose_plain.t2_name: The silence got too heavy to carry
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to feel like they're enough
prose_plain.t4_name: They're afraid of cracking something open
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard the healing promises before
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who actually gets relinquishment
prose_plain.implication: They've been offered the standard childhood-wound healing language before, and it slid right off them because it wasn't built for what they carry. The promises were too cheerful, too broad, too far from the specific feeling of being handed away by the person who was supposed to keep them. They don't distrust healing itself, they distrust that anyone selling it really understands what relinquishment does.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They light up when they hear from other adoptees who actually came through it, because that proves someone with the same original wound got better, not just someone with a hard childhood in general. They trust coaches who speak adoption language specifically, because that signals the person has gone deep enough into this world to be genuinely useful. And belonging to a community of people who share that same wound is part of what they're healing, so the community itself does some of the work.
prose_plain.push: They've felt dumped and empty and like they don't belong to anyone for long enough that carrying it in silence isn't working anymore.
prose_plain.pull: They want to stop feeling rejected by the story they were born into and start feeling like they're enough, even with that story attached to them.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that going straight at the birth-parent rejection will crack something open and leave them in worse shape than before they started.
prose_plain.habit: They've been keeping the 'I don't belong' feeling to themselves and steering around the whole subject rather than risk touching a wound that hasn't fully closed.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Take the friendships they already have and make them real
prose_plain.note: These buyers already know people. They have acquaintances. What they want is depth, not more names in their phone.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want someone to actually show up
prose_plain.t2_name: Whole weeks passed without real talk
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to feel chosen by someone
prose_plain.t4_name: They think they're the broken one
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried the advice, it flopped
prose_plain.t6_name: They need to feel understood first
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to join a club, say yes more, and put themselves out there. They tried some of it, it felt hollow and a little humiliating, and the friendships didn't get any deeper. So when they hear that kind of advice now, they're already gone before the second sentence works.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're carrying a private belief that this works for everyone except them, so hearing from real people who felt the same way and still made it work is the only thing that cracks that open. A voice that's warm and a little self-aware lowers the shame enough that they don't close the tab. And when they feel like they've worked in a room full of people who know exactly what friendless-at-30 feels like, they stop bracing and start actually reading.
prose_plain.push: They lost their friend group after a big life change and now whole weeks go by without a single real conversation.
prose_plain.pull: They want a way to deepen the friendships they already have that doesn't feel forced or embarrassing, something that could actually work for someone like them.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're starting to believe they're the reason it keeps failing, that something about them pushes people away and that's why they keep getting left on read.
prose_plain.habit: They stay home, they wait for other people to reach out first, and they scroll through other people's plans instead of making their own.

prose_plain.note: The person buying wants to save their relationship, not be a better parent.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop hurting their people
prose_plain.t2_name: The guilt stopped going away
prose_plain.t3_name: They want control before the snap
prose_plain.t4_name: They think it's just how they're wired
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried the tips already
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who gets anger specifically
prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'breathe through it' and 'pause before you react' more times than they can count, and they tried both, and the next blowup came anyway. The tips work fine in a calm moment but fall apart the second the real heat hits, which is the only moment that actually counts. So they're not skeptical of help in general, they're skeptical that anything works when the anger moves faster than the thinking does.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They carry a lot of shame about this, so they won't open up to someone who seems like a general stress coach with a few anger slides added in. They need to feel the person in front of them has gone deep into anger specifically, not wellness broadly. And when they see or hear from someone who was stuck in the exact same yell-apologise-repeat cycle and actually got out of it, that's what shifts their belief from 'this sounds good' to 'this might actually work for me.'
prose_plain.push: They keep snapping, feeling awful about it, promising themselves it won't happen again, and then it happens again, and that loop is tearing them apart.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel the anger rise and still keep it from flying out at the people they love most.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this isn't a habit they can change but just who they are, something baked in deep enough that no amount of work will touch it.
prose_plain.habit: They apologise after every blowup and they mean it every single time, and then they find themselves doing it again before the week is out.

prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who already vetted it
prose_plain.implication: They've been down the blog post and YouTube rabbit hole before and it felt like learning for a day or two. Then it didn't stick, and they couldn't tell if what they'd read was even accurate. They're not burned out on the subject, they're burned out on having no way to know what's solid and what's noise.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust their own judgement yet about what's worth reading, so they lean hard on whoever sounds like they've already done the vetting for them. A guide that looks crowd-tested feels safer than one person's recommendation, because one person could just be wrong. And if the person explaining it is warm and plain-spoken rather than cold and academic, they'll actually keep going instead of bouncing.
prose_plain.push: They keep making impulsive decisions they regret, and they want to stop. They also want to understand the field properly, but they don't know where to start and they can't tell what's worth their time versus what's just going to waste another evening.
prose_plain.pull: They want a curated, trustworthy set of books and courses that gives them a real foundation. Not another pile of open tabs. Something they can actually follow from one end to the other and feel like they've built something when they're done.
prose_plain.anxiety: They worry that without an economics background they won't be able to keep up. They also worry that teaching themselves won't be taken seriously by anyone else, that it won't count for anything outside their own head.
prose_plain.habit: They end up googling in circles, reading scattered articles, and closing the browser without having learned anything they can hold onto. It feels like progress while it's happening and then it's gone.

prose_plain.push: They go silent to avoid the fight, then the guilt builds heavy enough that they cave anyway and end up right back where they started.
prose_plain.pull: They want to hold a firm line with the people they're closest to and have it stay held, without the guilt that's always made them take it back before.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if they actually enforce it this time, the guilt will be unbearable or the relationship won't come back from it.
prose_plain.habit: They stop replying to buy themselves some space, then feel guilty enough to collapse back into doing whatever was asked of them, and the cycle starts over.

prose_plain.t1_name: They want to say no and stay okay
prose_plain.t2_name: They caved again and hated it
prose_plain.t3_name: They want the line to hold
prose_plain.t4_name: They expect guilt to wreck them
prose_plain.t5_name: They don't believe generic advice works
prose_plain.t6_name: They need proof the relationship survived
prose_plain.implication: They've read the boundary-setting posts, they've watched the videos, and they know the vocabulary cold. The advice they've gotten has always assumed the other person is a stranger or a reasonable adult, not someone they love and will sit across from at Christmas. So they've stopped trusting that what works in theory will hold when it's their mom on the phone and the guilt is already rising in their chest.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're watching to see whether anyone else's relationship actually survived what they're afraid of, because seeing that the family didn't fall apart is the only thing that makes trying feel survivable. They also need to feel like they've already moved, even a little, because one boundary they kept makes the next one feel less like a cliff edge. And when a coach sounds clinically grounded about why this happens, it pulls the guilt off them personally and gives them somewhere neutral to put it.
prose_plain.push: They've gone silent to avoid the fight, then felt guilty enough to cave anyway, and they're worn out from that cycle repeating every single time.
prose_plain.pull: They want to hold a firm line with the people they love and have it respected, without the guilt that's always dragged them back before.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if they actually enforce the limit, the guilt will be unbearable or the relationship won't come back from it.
prose_plain.habit: They stop replying to buy time, then the guilt builds until they collapse back into doing whatever was asked of them.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Set up systems so they and their team get more done with less chaos
prose_plain.note: These buyers want to work better as individuals or with a small team. They aren't trying to grow a company. They just want their days to run smoother.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to grow without breaking again
prose_plain.t2_name: Everything still runs through them
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to lead, not just grind
prose_plain.t4_name: They can't picture handing anything off
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard 'build SOPs' before
prose_plain.t6_name: They trust someone who's actually crossed over
prose_plain.implication: They've already consumed the standard advice: build SOPs, hire slow, document everything. None of it told them what to hand off first or how to know when they're actually ready to bring someone in, so they're still doing it all themselves and wondering if they're just not the kind of person who can delegate. The advice felt complete until they tried to use it, and then it fell apart.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't take direction from someone who hasn't made the freelancer-to-agency jump themselves, because they've already been burned by advice that sounded right but didn't hold up in practice. They need to see other businesses like theirs that scaled without something going wrong, because that specific fear is what's keeping them stuck. They're also already wired to follow a structured path, so when they see a staged progression they can commit to one step at a time, they lean in.
prose_plain.push: They're buried in work and scared of sliding back to that breaking point where nothing could move without them personally touching it.
prose_plain.pull: They want to stop grinding for every referral and start running something that reaches clients directly and doesn't depend entirely on them.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid of scaling before they're ready, bringing on someone too soon, or handing off work to someone who makes them look bad in front of a client.
prose_plain.habit: They do everything themselves because they genuinely can't see what someone else could take over without something going sideways.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me feel desirable again and comfortable in this body, and help me get close to someone without it feeling broken or strange.
prose_plain.note: These people are past the fear of dying. Now they want to feel like themselves again. The thing keeping them up at night has shifted from 'will I survive?' to 'will anyone want me?' and 'do I even want myself?'
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to feel like themselves again
prose_plain.t2_name: Treatment ended but fear didn't
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to feel wanted and whole
prose_plain.t4_name: Vigilance feels like the only protection
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing time helps
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who actually gets it
prose_plain.implication: They've been handed pamphlets, told to stay positive, and sent home like the hard part is over. The people who were supposed to help them told them anxiety is normal and time heals it, and neither of those things has turned out to be true. They've heard enough reassurance from people who don't feel what they feel, so gentle encouragement without real understanding bounces straight off them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust someone who hasn't lived close to what they've lived, so they buy from someone they genuinely like and believe actually understands them. They need to see other survivors who came out the other side feeling okay, because right now they can't picture that being possible for themselves. And because this work sits right next to their medical care, the coach has to feel credible enough to deserve a place at that table.
prose_plain.push: They're stuck in a limbo where chemo is done but life hasn't started back up, and the fear of the cancer returning runs in the background of every single day like an alarm they can't switch off.
prose_plain.pull: They want to watch a movie, plan a holiday, laugh with people they love, and feel like someone who just happens to have had cancer rather than someone who's still inside it.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that the moment they stop watching and worrying, that's exactly when the cancer comes back, so the constant vigilance feels like the only thing keeping them safe.
prose_plain.habit: They stay locked in high-alert mode, and some of them have reached for medication just to quiet the noise in their head, because that feels more manageable than trusting that it's actually okay to feel okay.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: They want to get through the day without being flattened by pain and exhaustion. And they want someone to finally take them seriously. That second part is huge. Because this illness doesn't show up on a scan, people around them often don't believe it's real. Doctors can be dismissive. Family can be worse. So when they're looking for help, they're not just looking for someone who can ease the symptoms. They're looking for someone who won't make them prove they're actually sick.
prose_plain.note: The core job is the same as with other chronic illness clients: manage the pain, get some life back. But with fibromyalgia and ME/CFS, being believed sits right at the centre of everything. These are conditions people have been told are in their head, sometimes for years. That history changes what your clients need from you before they'll trust you with anything else.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to be believed and still standing
prose_plain.t2_name: The illness started making every call
prose_plain.t3_name: They want their life back, not managed
prose_plain.t4_name: They've been dismissed one too many times
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped trusting people who help
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who already gets it
prose_plain.implication: They've been told it's stress, that a better mindset would fix it, that a new protocol would finally be the one. Doctors have sent them home with nothing and the wellness world has handed them systems that treated them like a puzzle to be solved rather than a person in pain. They're not cynical by nature, but being wrong about who to trust has cost them too much, too many times.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel safe fastest when the person in front of them is clearly one of them, or has spent enough real time with people like them that nothing needs to be explained from scratch. Other sick people still coping is the only proof they'll trust, because it's harder to fake than a certificate on a wall. Being genuinely understood isn't a nice extra for them, it's the reason they'd stay in the conversation at all.
prose_plain.push: The illness is running their life and they're watching friendships disappear while they fight it alone.

prose_plain.note: These parents want practical coordination, not help with a bitter ex. The focus is logistics: who has the kids when, how handoffs work, how two homes stay consistent.

prose_plain.t2_name: The ex made normal impossible
prose_plain.t3_name: They want the kids kept safe and steady
prose_plain.t4_name: They don't think it'll hold
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing cooperation comes
prose_plain.t6_name: They need proof it worked for someone
prose_plain.implication: They've already tried being reasonable, communicating more clearly, and waiting for the courts to do something. None of it changed how the ex behaves, and some of it gave the ex more room to maneuver. They're not interested in advice that assumes the other person will eventually come around, because they've watched that assumption fail them more than once.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're dealing with legal and emotional complexity that feels bigger than anything they've faced before, so they trust someone who clearly knows how these situations actually play out and can back that up with real badges or a track record. They also see themselves as the sane one, the parent who's trying to protect the kids, and they connect fast with anyone who obviously gets that and shares it. But what really tips them is hearing another parent say this is exactly what I did with an ex who wouldn't cooperate and here's what happened, because that's the only proof that feels real to them.
prose_plain.push: The ex won't cooperate and uses the kids to make things harder, and every time they try to fix it they come away more drained than before.
prose_plain.pull: They want the kids' lives to stay steady and both households to run without constant confusion, and they want that without it costing them their health, their money, or what's left of their sanity.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that even the right moves won't be enough, that the ex will find a way around any consequence again, and that pulling back or doing something different might somehow make things worse for the kids.
prose_plain.habit: They keep fighting, pleading, and over-explaining, putting in more effort on their end and hoping that eventually the ex will soften or the courts will step in and fix it.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop feeling like a fraud so I can own what I've earned and keep doing good work
prose_plain.note: These are people who are already succeeding. The fear isn't failure. It's being found out. They want to protect what they've built, and they already know imposter syndrome by name.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to own what they've earned
prose_plain.t2_name: They froze when a real opportunity came
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to feel worth knowing
prose_plain.t4_name: The mask feels safer than trying again
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing tips fix it
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's worn the mask
prose_plain.implication: They've done the affirmations, kept the journals, read the articles, and tried the confidence tricks, and none of it touched the thing underneath. What they were handed described a shinier, simpler problem than the one they actually live with every day. They're not cynical by nature, they're just tired, and they won't give their attention to anything that feels like another how-to list from someone who clearly hasn't been there.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They carry real shame about this, so they shut down fast when something feels clinical or preachy. Hearing other people like them, high-achieving, well-liked on the outside, talk honestly about the same hidden experience tells them they're not broken in some rare way. A coach who feels warm and human rather than distant and expert-y lowers the wall just enough for them to consider that this time could be different.
prose_plain.push: They tear themselves down before anyone else gets the chance, and that inner critic is loud enough to stop them going after things they actually want.
prose_plain.pull: They want to feel like someone worth knowing, someone who can go after what they want in relationships and in life without having to perform their way through every interaction.
prose_plain.anxiety: They've been trying to fix this since they were a teenager, and part of them has started to wonder if this is just who they are and who they'll always be.
prose_plain.habit: Wearing the mask is automatic now. The people-pleasing, the hidden jealousy, keeping the real version of themselves out of sight. It's uncomfortable, but it's familiar, and familiar feels safer than trying something again that might not work.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Build a team that runs the agency so they stop doing everything themselves
prose_plain.note: These people have already won clients on their own. Now they want to grow by hiring and leading people, not by working more hours.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop working for someone else
prose_plain.t2_name: The salary stopped feeling worth it
prose_plain.t3_name: They want clients and a real income
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared clients won't show up
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard the freedom promise before
prose_plain.t6_name: They trust someone who already did it
prose_plain.implication: They've been shown the 'quit your 9-5' dream so many times it doesn't work on them anymore. Every course, every ad, every Instagram post has made the same lifestyle promise, and they've stopped responding to it. What they haven't seen yet is someone showing them, in plain terms, how the clients actually come in and how the money actually replaces a salary.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're not moved by someone who looks successful, they're moved by someone who looks like them and got out. When they see real people who quit and aren't miserable, they believe it's possible because the person isn't a celebrity, they're just someone who was in the same spot. And when the coach has clearly done it themselves, that's not inspiration, that's evidence, and evidence is what finally shifts them.
prose_plain.push: They're underpaid, treated like they're replaceable, and they feel trapped selling their hours for a salary that doesn't reflect what they're actually worth.
prose_plain.pull: They want clients who pay well, the freedom to choose when they work, and they want to see real people who already made the jump and didn't end up crawling back.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they won't find enough clients to survive on, and that fear is what keeps them from fully committing, because going back to a full-time job feels like the worst thing that could happen to them.
prose_plain.habit: They stay in the salaried job because it feels safe, or they keep freelancing on the side without ever making the full leap, telling themselves they'll do it when the timing is right.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Find a real partner to build a life with, not just someone to spend time with.
prose_plain.note: These people aren't browsing. They want a committed relationship and a future family. That goal drives every decision they make.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want someone to build a life with
prose_plain.t2_name: The loneliness got too loud to ignore
prose_plain.t3_name: They want real love, not more hoping
prose_plain.t4_name: They think wanting it makes them pathetic
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard this will work before
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who gets the ache
prose_plain.implication: They've been through the apps, the listicles, the profile rewrites, and the advice from well-meaning friends, and none of it led anywhere real. Every new approach came with the feeling that this time would be different, and it wasn't, so they've stopped believing that different methods mean different results. They're not done wanting love, they're done trusting the things that claimed to deliver it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're carrying a quiet shame about how badly they want this, so they won't trust someone who feels slick or salesy, they need to feel genuinely seen first, and warmth gets through where badges don't. They also need to know that real people who felt exactly this stuck actually came out the other side, because their own track record has them doubting themselves. And because they've been burned by vague, generic advice, they need a coach who can say something specific about why what they do is different, something that holds up when they poke at it.
prose_plain.push: They're worn out from trying things that keep not working, and they're starting to wonder if wanting love this much makes them the problem.
prose_plain.pull: They want to find real love through something that doesn't feel like scrolling through a catalogue of disappointment.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid they'll do everything right and still end up alone, and they're ashamed that wanting love so badly feels like a weakness.
prose_plain.habit: They keep going back to dating apps even though the apps leave them feeling hollow, or they pull back from trying altogether and wait for something to change on its own.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop going in circles and make a decision they can actually live with.
prose_plain.note: Fear and regret drive this market, same as others. But the specific moment they want help with is being frozen. They aren't shopping for better thinking skills. They want out of the loop they are stuck in, right now.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to decide and stay decided
prose_plain.t2_name: The circles stopped feeling normal
prose_plain.t3_name: They want a call they can live with
prose_plain.t4_name: They don't trust their own judgement
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried the tips already
prose_plain.t6_name: They need proof it holds under doubt
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to trust their gut and write out the pros and cons, and they did both, and they still ended up awake at two in the morning replaying a choice they'd already made. The advice wasn't wrong exactly, it just had nothing to hold onto when the doubt came back. So they're not looking for another idea to try, they're looking for something that doesn't fall apart the second they feel uncertain again.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust their own thinking right now, so if someone with clear authority stands behind something, it gives them a reason to take it seriously that doesn't depend on their own shaky judgement. They're also the kind of person who makes a call and then walks it back when something feels off, so anything that helps them feel genuinely committed and consistent with what they already chose is a real relief to them. And when they see that other people who used to spiral just like them now make decisions and move on without the week of second-guessing, it tells them they're not broken, they just haven't had the right thing yet.
prose_plain.push: They can't stop second-guessing themselves, and even when they do land on something, they walk it back the moment any doubt shows up.
prose_plain.pull: They want to make a decision and actually hold it, without spending the next week wondering if they got it wrong.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that even a better process won't protect them from picking wrong and regretting it anyway.
prose_plain.habit: They loop through the same options over and over, never land cleanly on one, and then abandon the choice they did make once the doubt creeps back in.

prose_plain.implication: They've been told to trust their gut, make a list, weigh the options, sleep on it. They did all of it and still ended up awake at 2am replaying a call they already made. So they're not skeptical because they're difficult, they're skeptical because the things that were supposed to help didn't stop the spiral, and they don't want to waste time on something that leaves them in the same place.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Because they don't trust their own judgement right now, they need to see real authority behind whatever they're considering, someone who clearly knows what's going on, or they'll dismiss it before they give it a chance. They're also someone who makes a decision and then walks it back the moment doubt shows up, so anything that helps them feel genuinely committed and consistent is a relief to them, not a sales tactic. And when they see other people who used to loop just like they do now making calls and moving forward, it feels like proof they're not broken, just without the right support yet.
prose_plain.push: They can't stop second-guessing themselves, and when they do land on a call, they walk it back the moment something feels shaky.
prose_plain.pull: They want to make a decision and actually hold it, without spending the next week wondering if they got it wrong.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that even a better process won't protect them from picking wrong and regretting it anyway.
prose_plain.habit: They loop through the same options over and over, never land on one cleanly, and then walk away from the choice they did make as soon as doubt creeps back in.

prose_plain.push: After six-plus years of trying, they keep going back to food when things get hard, and every binge pulls them into a spiral of negative thinking they can't reason their way out of.
prose_plain.pull: They want to reach a point where a hard day is just a hard day, where food is ordinary and the shame doesn't follow them into the next morning.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this really is a self-control problem, and because every attempt has failed them so far, they're convinced they'll be the one person nothing can help.
prose_plain.habit: When distress hits they reach for food to feel better, and when the guilt follows they go back to strict rules, which sets the whole thing off again.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Make peace with food and learn to trust their own hunger again
prose_plain.note: These buyers aren't in crisis. They have already decided intuitive eating is the right path for them. They come in hopeful, not desperate. They want to grow into something better, not escape something terrible. That changes how you talk to them. Lead with possibility, not pain.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop hurting around food
prose_plain.t2_name: The guilt hit harder than the binge did
prose_plain.t3_name: They want a rough day to just be a rough day
prose_plain.t4_name: They think they're the one it won't fix
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard the promise too many times
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who can explain why
prose_plain.implication: They've been told the answer is more willpower, a cleaner plan, or a softer version of the same restriction they've already tried. Every time it held for a bit, then the binge came back harder, and they ended up with more shame than they started with. They don't distrust one program, they distrust all of them, because their own life keeps showing them the promise doesn't hold.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've spent years telling themselves they're weak, so they need someone who can explain clearly why the restricting made the bingeing worse, because the cycle was doing it, not their character. They also need to see real people who were in the exact same place and actually got out, because without that they assume everyone else improved and they're the exception.
prose_plain.push: They've been trying for six-plus years, and every hard day ends the same way: they eat to get through it, the guilt rushes in, the rules get tighter, and that pressure builds until the next binge hits worse than the one before.
prose_plain.pull: They want to get to a place where food doesn't carry shame, where a bad day is just a bad day, and where they can trust what their own body is telling them about hunger.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared the real explanation is that they have no self-control, and since nothing has stuck yet they're starting to believe they're the one person this genuinely won't work for.
prose_plain.habit: When distress shows up they reach for food because it's the only thing that brings fast relief, and when the guilt kicks in they go straight back to strict rules, which builds the pressure that makes the next binge worse.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Learn how to support my loved one's recovery without making it worse
prose_plain.note: The buyer is the parent or carer, not the person in recovery. They act out of love and fear. They want to help but they are terrified of doing the wrong thing and setting things back.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their loved one to survive
prose_plain.t2_name: They kept making things worse
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to help without hurting
prose_plain.t4_name: They don't know what's safe
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried doing the right thing
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who gets families
prose_plain.implication: They've read the articles, watched the documentaries, and tried tough love and then soft love and then boundaries and then no boundaries. Every approach came with a promise that if they just did it consistently, things would turn around. None of it did, and now they half-expect that any new help is just another version of the same advice wearing different clothes.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're carrying a lot of shame about things they said or did before they understood addiction, so they need someone who can explain clearly why those things didn't work without making them feel like a bad person. They also need to see other families who looked as lost as they feel right now and came out the other side, because without that proof they assume their situation is the one that's too far gone.
prose_plain.push: They've tried being firm, tried being gentle, tried saying nothing, and every approach either started a fight or pushed their loved one further away, and now they're scared that whatever they do next will make things worse again.
prose_plain.pull: They want to get to a place where they can have a conversation with their loved one without it going sideways, where they feel like they're actually helping instead of just hoping they're not doing damage.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that they've already said or done too much, that the relationship is too damaged, and that even with the right support they're too far behind to make any real difference now.
prose_plain.habit: When things feel out of control they either step in hard and try to manage everything, or they go completely quiet and wait, and neither one feels right and both leave them lying awake running through what they should have done instead.

prose_plain.note: People in this market already know Amazon FBA exists. They have seen the ads, watched the videos, and heard the promises. They aren't new to the idea. They're deciding who to trust and whether it will actually work for them.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their store to actually sell
prose_plain.t2_name: Their money started running out
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to know what's broken
prose_plain.t4_name: They've tried things and stayed stuck
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped trusting general advice
prose_plain.t6_name: They need proof it worked for someone like them
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to drive more traffic, run promotions, be patient, and keep posting. They did all of it and their bank account kept shrinking anyway. So when they hear general advice now, they tune it out, because they've already lived what happens when they follow it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're scared and a little desperate, so they're not handing trust to just anyone who sounds confident. They need to see that someone has already fixed this for a store that looked exactly like theirs, because that's the only evidence that feels real when they're this close to quitting. And because they're low on money and high on doubt, getting something genuinely useful before they spend anything is the only thing that makes them feel safe enough to take one more step.
prose_plain.push: They have traffic and saves but almost no orders, and their money is running out with no other income coming in.
prose_plain.pull: They want a clear, specific reason why visitors aren't buying and a real way to fix it without spending more on ads.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid the whole thing is failing and that they'll have to walk away from it entirely.
prose_plain.habit: When things feel stuck, they throw a little money at a promotion and then wait and hope instead of finding out what's actually stopping people from buying.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me have the hard conversation without it turning into a fight or something I keep putting off.
prose_plain.note: People here want a specific skill. They already know this kind of help exists and they have seen plenty of options. They aren't trying to figure out if this is for them. They're trying to figure out who to trust with it.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop coming across as angry
prose_plain.t2_name: It came out wrong again
prose_plain.t3_name: They want people to actually know them
prose_plain.t4_name: They think they're wired this way
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried being vulnerable before
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who can explain it
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to 'just communicate' and to 'be vulnerable' and they tried it and it blew up or fell flat. Generic advice left them feeling more broken, not less, because it didn't tell them what to do with the feeling before it turned into something they regretted. They're not looking for encouragement anymore, they want someone who can explain what's actually happening inside them and show them how to practice it until it sticks.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They already believe emotional skills can be learned, so they're looking for someone who clearly knows this territory well and can prove they've helped people who shut down the same way they do. Real examples of people who used to go silent and now don't reassure them it's possible for someone with their exact history. They also respond to small, concrete steps because finishing each one gives them proof they're actually changing, not just reading about changing.
prose_plain.push: They can't get their feelings out even with people they're close to, and when they finally do say something, it comes out as anger, which makes them feel like that's just who they are.
prose_plain.pull: They want the people around them to actually know how they're feeling, and they want to feel like someone who handles their emotions well instead of someone who buries them until it's too late.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid how they are with emotions goes all the way back to childhood or old relationships, and that it's already too late to change something that deep.
prose_plain.habit: Staying quiet and closed off is what they've always done, and silence is already their automatic response before they've consciously decided anything.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Share my home again with my adult child without losing the peace and space I had when they left
prose_plain.note: These parents had tasted freedom. Then a grown kid moved back in. The work isn't about welcoming them home. It's about keeping the rules clear and holding onto what they built for themselves once the house was quiet.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their own life back
prose_plain.t2_name: They ran out of self completely
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to feel full again
prose_plain.t4_name: They think it's too late now
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard 'rediscover yourself' before
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who actually gets it
prose_plain.implication: They've been handed soft encouragement and vision board exercises more times than they can count, and none of it looked like a real life they could actually step into. It all felt like being patted on the head by someone who didn't quite understand what they'd lost. So they scroll past anything that sounds like that now because they've already been disappointed by it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel like the only person in the world sitting in this particular kind of lonely, so seeing someone else who lived it and came out the other side is the first thing that makes them think it's actually possible for them. They're also too worn down to trust anyone who feels cold or preachy, so warmth and real understanding are what make them stay instead of clicking away.
prose_plain.push: They gave everything to their child for years and now they don't have friends, don't have relationships, and don't know who they are when parenting isn't the only thing filling their days.
prose_plain.pull: They're reaching for a life that feels genuinely happy and full, one that belongs to them and runs on their own wants instead of someone else's needs.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid it's too late to build something real, and they worry that moving toward their own life somehow means they're moving away from their child.
prose_plain.habit: They keep pouring their focus back into their child even now, because parenting has been the only role they've known for so long that stepping outside it feels terrifying.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me keep earning, stay connected to people, and hold some kind of routine while I live and work from anywhere, without wearing myself down or feeling like I have no home.
prose_plain.note: These people chose this life on purpose. They have already tried tools, communities, and routines. They aren't looking to be sold on the idea of working remotely. They're past that. What they want now is to make it last without burning out or feeling unmoored. Speak to sustainability, not the dream.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to feel at home somewhere
prose_plain.t2_name: The loneliness got too heavy
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to belong somewhere real
prose_plain.t4_name: They've tried the obvious stuff already
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped trusting generic advice
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's been there
prose_plain.implication: They've already read the culture shock articles and they know the word for what they're feeling. That knowledge hasn't moved anything for them, so they're done with content that names the problem and then stops. They're looking for someone who has an actual path through it, not another label for the wall they're already staring at.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They carry a quiet fear that they're the only one who can't crack this, so hearing that other people felt exactly this and came out the other side is what actually softens that fear. They don't trust a coach who sounds clinical or detached, because the wound is personal and they need to feel the coach knows this feeling from the inside. When they sense that someone genuinely gets the homesick, adrift feeling firsthand, trust comes fast.
prose_plain.push: They're lonely in a way that's hard to explain to people back home, cut off from their usual friendships, exhausted from pretending they're fine, and some days they're convinced moving was a mistake.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know how long this actually takes and what they can do right now to start feeling settled and connected, instead of just waiting for things to improve on their own.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that belonging is something that will keep slipping away from them, that they've already tried the obvious things and nothing worked, and that they're going to spend their whole time abroad feeling like an outsider.
prose_plain.habit: They pull back from new situations, spend a lot of time in their own head replaying what they miss, and keep coming back to the idea of just going home rather than pushing through to something better.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me get settled, stay healthy, and feel safe retiring in another country.
prose_plain.note: What drives these buyers isn't about fitting in socially. It's about feeling secure and comfortable as they age.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to finally feel at home
prose_plain.t2_name: The loneliness got too heavy to ignore
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to belong somewhere again
prose_plain.t4_name: They think they've already tried everything
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing time fixes it
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's lived it
prose_plain.implication: They've read the articles, watched the videos, and heard the advice about culture shock plenty of times. They already know what to call the feeling, and that knowledge hasn't moved them an inch closer to feeling settled. What they've been handed are labels and lists, and they're done with anything that names the wall without showing them a way through it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They carry a quiet fear that everyone else figured this out except them, so hearing that real expats felt exactly this lost and came through it is the thing that actually loosens that fear. They won't trust someone who sounds polished and distant, because this hurt is personal and they need to feel the coach has been in the same cold water. When they sense that, trust comes fast.
prose_plain.push: They're lonely in a way that's hard to explain to anyone back home, cut off from the friendships that used to hold them up, and worn out from pretending they're fine. Some days they're convinced the move was a mistake and going home is the only honest option left.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know how long this actually takes and what they can do right now to start feeling connected instead of just waiting and hoping things get better on their own.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that belonging is something that's always going to be just out of reach for them, that they've already tried the obvious things and none of it worked, and that they'll spend their whole time abroad feeling like an outsider who never quite fits.
prose_plain.habit: They pull back from new situations instead of stepping into them, spend long stretches inside their own head replaying what they've lost, and keep circling back to the idea of just going home rather than pushing through to something better.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Reach out and fix things without getting hurt again
prose_plain.note: These people want to get back together. They aren't looking for ways to live apart. What pulls them forward is the hope of repairing the bond, not escaping it.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop feeling like a bad person
prose_plain.t2_name: Talking to family kept making things worse
prose_plain.t3_name: They want a guilt-free life away from this
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared digging in makes it worse
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard 'boundaries' and felt nothing
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's seen this before
prose_plain.implication: They've been through therapy that pushed them toward reconciliation and came out feeling worse about themselves. They've been told to set boundaries and practice self-care so many times those phrases have stopped meaning anything. What they haven't found yet is someone who tells them clearly that choosing distance can be the healthy thing, and who actually helps them stop feeling like a monster for doing it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've spent years being told by their own family that they're broken, so they need someone with real badges to say plainly that they're not. They also feel completely alone in what they've done, and hearing from other people who made the same choice and are living well is the first thing that lets them breathe. Other people's stories of guilt-free estrangement don't just comfort them, they're the closest thing to proof that a peaceful life on the other side is real.
prose_plain.push: Every time they talk to their family their mental health gets worse, not better, and they know it.
prose_plain.pull: They've had glimpses of a happy life away from their family and they want to get there without guilt pulling them back.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared people will see them as someone who abandoned elderly parents, and they're also scared that looking closely at the shame will make everything feel heavier than it already does.
prose_plain.habit: They cycle back into contact when the guilt gets too loud, or they stay stuck replaying shame and never fully let themselves move forward.

prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop feeling like the bad person

What they haven't found is someone who says outright that choosing distance can be the healthy thing, and who actually helps them feel less like a monster for considering it.

But badges alone don't do it. Hearing from people who made the same choice and came out the other side without regret is the closest thing to proof they have that a guilt-free life is actually possible, not just something people say.
prose_plain.push: Every time they talk to their family their mental health gets worse, and they know it, and they keep noticing it.
prose_plain.pull: They've caught glimpses of what a calmer life could feel like, and they want to get there without guilt pulling them back every time they get close.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared people will see them as someone who abandoned their elderly parents, and they're also scared that digging into the shame will make everything feel heavier than it already does.
prose_plain.habit: When the guilt gets loud enough they cycle back into contact just to quiet it, or they stay frozen, replaying shame over and over, and never fully let themselves move forward either way.

prose_plain.note: These people are grieving. That's the heart of it. They aren't trying to feel okay about being apart. They're trying to make sense of a loss that has no funeral, no closure, and no end.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop feeling like a bad person
prose_plain.t2_name: Talking to family kept making things worse
prose_plain.t3_name: They want a guilt-free life away from family
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared digging in makes it worse

prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who says distance is okay
prose_plain.implication: They've sat through therapy that nudged them toward reconciliation and walked out feeling like the problem. They've been handed 'set boundaries' and 'practice self-care' so many times those phrases now make them tired before they've even started. What they haven't found yet is someone who says out loud that choosing distance can be the healthy choice, and who actually helps them feel like a decent person for making it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've spent years being told they're broken by the very people who broke them, so they need someone with real badges to say otherwise before they'll trust anything. They also feel like the only person who's ever walked away from a parent, and hearing that other people did it and don't regret it is the first thing that makes them feel less like a freak. Other people's stories of life after estrangement aren't just comforting to them, they're the closest thing to proof they have that a guilt-free life is actually possible.
prose_plain.push: Every time they get back in contact with their family their mental health gets worse, and they know it, and they go back anyway because the guilt gets louder than the pain.
prose_plain.pull: They've had glimpses of what a calm, happy life could look like away from the family, and they want to get all the way there without guilt pulling them back every time they get close.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared people will see them as someone who abandoned elderly parents, and they're also scared that actually looking at the shame will make everything feel heavier than it already does.
prose_plain.habit: They cycle back into contact when the guilt gets too loud to ignore, or they stay stuck replaying old shame and never let themselves fully move forward into the life they're trying to build.

prose_plain.note: What these women want most is relief from pain and grief. They aren't looking for tips on getting pregnant. They're trying to survive loss.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want a baby and to survive the waiting

prose_plain.implication: They've been told IVF is the answer, and they've sat through the injections and the waiting rooms and the phone calls, and it still didn't work. They've been handed normal lab results so many times that a clean bill of health doesn't feel like good news anymore, it feels like a dead end. When something sounds like everything they've already been promised, they stop reading.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They need to hear from a real woman who lost more than one pregnancy and came out the other side, because a stranger's honest story reaches them when polished claims don't. They're trying to understand medical complexity that no one has fully explained to them, so they need to feel confident that whoever they're talking to genuinely knows this territory. They're exhausted and raw, and they won't stay anywhere that feels cold or procedural, so warmth isn't a bonus for them, it's what keeps them in the room.
prose_plain.push: They've watched years go by and sat through failed IVF rounds, and the fear that their window is closing is sitting on top of everything else they're carrying.
prose_plain.pull: They're looking for a way to try again that doesn't put them back on the exact same road that already let them down.
prose_plain.anxiety: Their labs all came back fine, and that scares them, because if nothing is technically wrong, they don't know what's left to fix or where to go next.
prose_plain.habit: They keep returning to clinical-only routes, repeating the same cycles and waiting on the same systems, even when those systems haven't given them what they need.

They don't think the advice was wrong exactly, they think there's something broken in them that stops them from following it.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've already decided they want to save, so when something asks for a small, automatic commitment instead of daily willpower, it fits how they already think about themselves. They're also carrying real shame about giving up before, so they warm up fast to a voice that doesn't treat the occasional treat as a moral failure. prose_plain.pull: They want spending to slow down and saving to build up without having to fight themselves over every single purchase.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if they get too strict with themselves they'll tip over into being stingy, and lose the small pleasures that make ordinary life feel good.
prose_plain.habit: They read books and blogs, they build a budget, they feel hopeful for a few weeks, and then it collapses and they slide straight back into the spending patterns they were trying to leave behind.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get through losing their partner and figure out who they are and how to live without them
prose_plain.note: When a spouse dies, the person left behind loses more than company. They lose the role they built their life around. That makes this grief different. They need to work out how to be alone and who they even are now.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop feeling hollow inside
prose_plain.t2_name: The emptiness got too heavy to carry
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to grieve all the way through
prose_plain.t4_name: Everyone around them says move on
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing anyone can help
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's been here
prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'give it time' and 'stay busy' and 'they'd want you to be happy' more times than they can count, and none of it touched the actual pain. The people who said it meant well, but what they heard was that their grief was too big, going on too long, becoming a problem. So they've stopped expecting real help and started wondering if feeling this way is just what the rest of their life looks like.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel completely alone in this, like no one around them is actually carrying what they're carrying, so when they find someone who works with people exactly like them or has been through it themselves, something in them relaxes fast. A warm, real presence earns their trust in a way that a polished, clinical expert never would. They're also scared they're grieving wrong, so a little steady reassurance that what they're feeling is normal is enough to make them lean in.
prose_plain.push: They feel hollow without the person they lost and they're stuck in mourning with no idea how to move through it.
prose_plain.pull: They want to let themselves grieve all the way through and land somewhere that feels like acceptance, without that meaning they've forgotten who they lost.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid they'll feel this way forever, and they're afraid the people around them are right that the grief has gone on too long.
prose_plain.habit: They keep pushing the grief down because everyone around them is signaling that it's time to be over it, so they stay stuck instead of moving through it.

prose_plain.note: These men aren't just looking for self-acceptance. They want the people around them to accept them too. Fear of being seen as less of a man, by others, not just themselves, is what drives the search for help.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop losing people they love
prose_plain.t2_name: A friend left and named them as the reason
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to stay present without wrecking things
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared progress is just another mask
prose_plain.t5_name: They've already been told they're not broken
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who has lived it
prose_plain.implication: They've already found the HSP label and read all the things that said they're not broken, not too much, not wrong. That felt like relief for about a week, and then Tuesday morning arrived and nothing had actually changed. They're not looking for more permission to exist, they're looking for something that shifts how it feels inside their body when the world gets loud.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They trust a coach who says 'we' and means it, because most of their life they've been the one person in the room who felt too much and said too much and got left out for it. They also need to know the person they're paying has been inside this kind of overwhelm, not just read about it, because studied empathy reads as fake to them almost immediately. And when a coach can talk about sensitivity in a way that sounds grounded and backed by something real, it gives them permission to take the work seriously instead of wondering if they're just buying comfort.
prose_plain.push: A friend left and told them their oversensitivity and drama were the reason, even though their intentions were good the whole time.
prose_plain.pull: They want to stay regulated and present when things get hard, so their relationships stop paying the price for how deeply they feel everything.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that whatever they learn will just sit on top of who they are like a costume, and that underneath it they'll still be too much, or that getting better means becoming someone they don't recognise.
prose_plain.habit: When they're overwhelmed they go inward and apologise, over and over, without having anything that actually moves the feeling through them.

prose_plain.note: These buyers have already decided to stay. They aren't weighing their options. They want to know how to actually do the work of rebuilding. They come in looking for a clear path forward, not a reason to try.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want the pain to have meant something
prose_plain.t2_name: The ground went out from under them
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to know the marriage can survive
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared trust can't really come back
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing generic advice helps
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who has done this
prose_plain.implication: They've been told that time heals everything and that better communication fixes most things, and neither of those touched what's actually happening inside them. This doesn't feel like a rough patch or a normal problem, so advice built for normal problems sounds hollow to someone replaying a three-year lie in their head. They're not cynical, they're just very specific now about what kind of help they need.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're in shock and they can't trust their own judgement right now, so they need to feel certain the person guiding them has walked other couples through exactly this kind of betrayal, not just relationship trouble in general. Hearing that real people healed from this specific thing is the only thing that makes hope feel possible instead of foolish. And they won't open up to someone who doesn't feel warm and safe, because their trust has already been destroyed once and they're not risking it again without a good reason.
prose_plain.push: They found out their partner had been cheating, sometimes for years, and everything they thought was solid turned out not to be.
prose_plain.pull: They want to know whether healing is actually possible, whether the relationship can survive, and what the real steps look like to get to either answer.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that trust can't really come back, and that if they try and it doesn't work, all the pain they've already been through will have been for nothing.
prose_plain.habit: They're stuck replaying the discovery over and over, frozen in shock, unable to figure out what to do next or even where to start looking.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Handle screen time for my neurodivergent child when the usual rules make things worse and screens sometimes actually help
prose_plain.note: Parents here have already tried the standard advice and it failed. They know their child's needs are specific. They aren't looking for basics. They want someone who gets that screens aren't simply bad or good for their kid.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their child safe from harm
prose_plain.t2_name: Their toddler seemed already addicted
prose_plain.t3_name: They want peace without the screaming
prose_plain.t4_name: Taking it away makes things worse
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried the timer approach already
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who sounds clinical
prose_plain.implication: They've read the screen time articles. They've set the limits and downloaded the apps and tried holding firm, and none of it worked the way it was supposed to. They don't trust a version of that same advice they haven't heard before, because the screaming that came after they held firm was worse than the screen was.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're scared they've already damaged a developing brain, so they move fast toward anyone who sounds like a child development expert rather than a parenting blogger with opinions. They also need to see other parents who had the same addicted-toddler fear and came through it, because without that they assume their child's situation is too far gone to fix. The clock feels real to them too, a 19-month-old's brain feels like a window that's closing, and that urgency means they act quickly when something finally sounds credible.
prose_plain.push: Their child looks addicted at 19 months old, and they're scared the damage is already done at an age when it shouldn't be reversible.
prose_plain.pull: They want a way to wean their child off screens and undo what's happened, without a daily battle they don't have the energy to fight.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid the harm to their child's brain is already permanent, and they're also afraid that taking the screen away just makes the meltdowns louder and harder than the screen ever was.
prose_plain.habit: They hand the device over because it's the only thing that buys five quiet minutes, and in that moment the quiet wins every time.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me feel real and seen in an identity that straight people and gay people both pretend doesn't exist.
prose_plain.note: What these people need most is to feel their identity is real. The fear isn't mainly about coming out safely. It's about being erased by both sides.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to be known and still loved
prose_plain.t2_name: Hiding it started breaking them
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to come out and stay safe

prose_plain.implication: They've been told to just be themselves so many times that the advice has gone hollow. It was never wrong, but it never told them what to say, how to pace it, or how to stay physically and emotionally safe while doing it. They're not looking for encouragement anymore, they're looking for something concrete that takes real consequences seriously.

When they see someone who looked exactly like them, closeted and convinced it would go badly, come out and keep their relationships intact, the whole thing starts to feel survivable. They trust a coach who's guided people through this before because the stakes feel too high to figure it out alone.
prose_plain.push: They're having panic attacks and carrying chronic stress because they're still hiding who they are every single day.
prose_plain.pull: They want the relief of being fully known and still loved, without carrying the secret anymore.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're convinced the people they love will be disappointed, pull away, or that being honest will put them somewhere unsafe.
prose_plain.habit: They keep presenting as straight because staying hidden has felt like the less dangerous option for so long that it's become automatic.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Stop carrying the damage a narcissistic parent left behind and break the patterns it set in motion for life
prose_plain.note: The person who hurt them is a parent, not an ex. The harm started in childhood and shaped who they became. This isn't about getting over a relationship. It's about undoing something that got built into them.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to feel real and whole again
prose_plain.t2_name: No contact didn't stop the pain
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to stop needing approval
prose_plain.t4_name: They expect to cave again
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing recovery works
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who already knows
prose_plain.implication: They've been told no contact is the answer, and they did it, and the obsessive thoughts kept coming anyway. They've been told time heals this, but months later they're still checking the ex's profile and blaming themselves for everything. The standard advice feels like it was written for a normal breakup, not for someone whose sense of self was hollowed out long before any relationship started.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They've felt so confused and wrong for so long that when a coach names exactly what's happening inside them, it's the first time they've felt sane, and that kind of precision builds trust faster than anything else. They've stopped responding to general success stories because they're convinced their damage is different, so the only proof they believe comes from someone who was also discarded and actually got better. Being in a group of people who share that specific wound is the first real relief they've felt, because being understood by someone who lived the same thing is something they haven't had before.
prose_plain.push: They tried no contact and it didn't quiet anything. The pain is just as loud weeks or months later, and that scares them because they thought cutting contact was the fix.
prose_plain.pull: They want the ex out of their head for good and they want to feel like a real person again, someone with worth who doesn't go looking for approval to feel okay.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared they'll cave around the three-week mark like they always have, and even more scared that nothing will ever actually work for someone as damaged as they feel.
prose_plain.habit: They ruminate, they check the ex's social media, they run the same self-blame loops over and over, and even though it hurts every time, it feels like the only thread still connecting them to something that once felt real.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Handle tense conversations calmly so I stop avoiding them and keep the relationship intact
prose_plain.note: People come to you because conflict makes them anxious, not because they want to win. They want the dread to go away. They want to keep the relationship. That's what they are paying for.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop folding under pressure
prose_plain.t2_name: They caved and regretted it
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to push back without blowing up
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared the other person leaves angry
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried the tactics and froze
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who feels safe to them
prose_plain.implication: They've read the negotiation explainers and watched the breakdown videos, and every bit of it assumed they were already comfortable sitting in tension with another person. They're not, and they knew it, so they filed it away as something that works for people who aren't wired like them. By now they don't believe the standard advice applies to them at all.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: Their gut has told them to cave in every high-stakes moment they can remember, so they don't trust it and they need a method that feels solid and comes from someone who clearly knows what they're doing. They also need to have decided their limit before the conversation starts, because once they're in it their instinct is to fold and apologise. When the approach feels calm and friendly rather than aggressive, it stops sounding like something that'll wreck the relationship, which is the fear that's been keeping them quiet.
prose_plain.push: They said yes when they meant no, or accepted the first number without a word, and now they're replaying it and wishing they'd held their ground.
prose_plain.pull: They want to ask for more and actually get it, without spending days dreading the conversation before it even happens.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that the moment they push back, the other person gets angry, thinks badly of them, or walks away for good.
prose_plain.habit: They take the first offer, they go quiet when something feels wrong, and they tell themselves they're just being easy to work with.

prose_plain.note: The fight is specifically about screens and social media, but the parent buying is the same parent you already know
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their daughter back
prose_plain.t2_name: She stopped talking to them
prose_plain.t3_name: They want real conversations again
prose_plain.t4_name: They're afraid they caused this
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried firm limits already
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who explains why
prose_plain.implication: They've already been told to set firm boundaries, stay consistent, and take the phone away. They did those things. The distance just got wider and the fights got worse. So when they hear that kind of advice now, they don't feel hopeful, they feel tired, because they've already been down that road and it led nowhere.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're carrying a quiet belief that they somehow broke their kid, so they need an expert who tells them plainly that this isn't what bad parenting looks like, because they won't let themselves believe that on their own. They also need to hear that other parents who love their kids and tried hard have been in this exact spot and found their way through, because that's the only thing that makes hope feel real instead of foolish. And they'll shut down the moment they feel even slightly judged, because they're already saying the harshest things to themselves every single day.
prose_plain.push: Their daughter was doing fine, and then over the past year she wasn't, and nothing they've tried has brought her back to them.
prose_plain.pull: They want a real conversation with her again, one where she actually opens up instead of walking away or shutting down.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid that trying one more thing will just become more proof that they've been getting it wrong all along.
prose_plain.habit: They keep reaching for punishment because it feels like action, even though they already know in their gut that it's making things worse.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me see how growing up in that house made me who I am, so I can stop doing the same things over and over.
prose_plain.note: Many of these people are still early in figuring out why they feel the way they do. They have just started connecting their childhood to their current problems. They aren't yet looking for a solution. They're looking for an explanation.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop giving themselves away
prose_plain.t2_name: The exhaustion finally broke through
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to understand why they're like this
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared people will leave them
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing awareness is enough
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who explains the why
prose_plain.implication: They've read the books, they know the word codependency, and they've tried saying no at least once. Every bit of help they've found has sat on the surface, telling them to just set a boundary as if that habit isn't wired into them from before they could name it. They've been told that knowing the pattern would break it, and it didn't, so they're not convinced anything goes deep enough to actually change how they're built.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They feel less broken when they're around others who grew up as the accommodating one in the house, because it stops feeling like a personal flaw and starts feeling like something that was done to them. They trust someone who can explain why their nervous system works this way, not just that it does, because that's the first explanation that makes change feel possible rather than just desirable. And when they say no once and the world doesn't fall apart, their brain starts to question the story they've carried since childhood about who they have to be to stay loved.
prose_plain.push: They're burnt out from giving to everyone around them, and socialising feels like a performance they're already tired of before it starts.
prose_plain.pull: They want to understand why they keep ending up in the same patterns, learn to say no without a flood of guilt, and stop handing themselves over to relationships that leave them empty.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if they stop people-pleasing, the people they love will leave, and they're scared they'll end up in another draining relationship even after doing all the work.
prose_plain.habit: Saying yes is automatic for them, it started in childhood, and it doesn't feel like a choice, it feels like who they are.

prose_plain.implication: They've been told to lower the bar, embrace imperfection, and stop caring so much. prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't listen to someone who seems soft on quality, so they need to see real badges before they'll believe a word. prose_plain.push: They're stuck, missing deadlines, and burning out because their own standards have become a trap they can't get out of.
prose_plain.pull: They want to act, finish things, and hand in work without the constant grinding feeling that it's still not good enough.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if they ease up even a little, they'll slide into mediocrity and people will finally see they weren't that good to begin with.
prose_plain.habit: They over-polish, they stall, or they don't start at all because starting something imperfect feels worse than not starting.
