prose_plain.jtbd_job: Get my teen to stop vaping before it damages their brain and ruins their future
prose_plain.note: The person buying is the parent, not the teen. They're scared and protective. Most parents in this market are still figuring out that help even exists, so you can't assume they already know what to do or where to turn.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their kid safe and free
prose_plain.t2_name: Their teen's health scared them badly
prose_plain.t3_name: They want their kid's future back
prose_plain.t4_name: They don't think anything will work
prose_plain.t5_name: They've heard every promise already
prose_plain.t6_name: They trust someone who gets it
prose_plain.implication: These parents have already tried things. They've talked to doctors, downloaded apps, read articles, maybe tried patches or gum themselves so they'd understand what their kid was going through, and none of it stuck. Every method came wrapped in a promise, and every relapse left them more convinced the problem is their kid, or themselves, not the method. They're not open to a new solution the way a fresh buyer is. They need to see why this is different before they'll let themselves hope.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're carrying a heavy load of shame, and they'll tune out anyone who makes them feel like they failed their kid or were naive to miss the signs. The only voice they'll actually hear is someone who doesn't talk down to them and who has seen parents exactly like them come through this. They also need to see real families, not success stories that sound too clean, because when they see an ordinary parent who was just as scared and just as stuck, quitting starts to feel possible instead of just something other people manage to do.
prose_plain.push: Their teen is visibly hooked, and the health scares are real enough now that they can't tell themselves it'll sort itself out.
prose_plain.pull: They want their kid free of the addiction for good, not just cutting back, and they want to stop feeling like helpless bystanders in their own home.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that whatever they try will blow up the relationship with their teen, that their kid will just hide it better, or that one bad week at school will wipe out any progress.
prose_plain.habit: Their teen reaches for the vape without even thinking, and when these parents try to bring it up they hear the same fight start before they've finished the sentence, so a lot of the time they don't bring it up at all.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Retire without running out of money, even if they feel behind.
prose_plain.note: These are everyday savers following the standard advice: contribute to a 401(k), hope for the best. They aren't obsessing over early retirement math or optimizing every dollar. They want to feel safe, not smart.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to stop being afraid of retirement
prose_plain.t2_name: The fear got too loud to ignore
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to know they'll be okay
prose_plain.t4_name: They think they're already too far behind
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing the math works for them
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's seen their exact situation
prose_plain.implication: They've read the articles, they know what a savings rate is, and they've probably made a budget more than once. What they don't believe anymore is that the standard advice applies to someone at their age and starting point, because nobody has ever shown them the numbers for their specific life. They've filed it under 'that's for people who started earlier,' and that belief is sticky.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: The stakes are their entire financial future, so they won't trust someone who just sounds confident. They need to see a real track record or verifiable badges before they'll listen at all, and they scan hard for people who were in the same hole they're in now, because that's the only proof that feels true to them.
prose_plain.push: They're scared, and some of them have almost nothing saved and no clear path forward. The fear that they may never get to stop working sits with them every single day.
prose_plain.pull: They want to reach financial independence in a defined number of years, or at least retire comfortably without spending their last decade dreading what's coming.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that past false starts and poor financial choices have already decided their future, and that trying again at this point won't be enough to change where they end up.
prose_plain.habit: They avoid looking at the numbers directly. They've tried before, lost the thread, and haven't fully committed to a system that holds, so they stay one step away from the full picture.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me turn my service record and years of moving around into a civilian career that pays me what I'm worth.
prose_plain.note: These people feel like outsiders the moment they leave the military. They've done hard, real work, but civilian employers don't always see it that way. They want someone who gets that world and can speak for them inside it. They trust coaches who've lived it or who clearly understand it. They're deeply loyal to people in their corner.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to feel safe going back
prose_plain.t2_name: Staying out got scarier than going back

prose_plain.implication: They've been handed the same advice so many times it's lost all weight. Update the resume, rehearse the pitch, believe in yourself. They've heard it from every direction and none of it touched the fear in their chest, so now when they hear it again it sounds like noise. They're not waiting for more tips. They're waiting for someone who names what's actually going on inside them.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't believe going back is possible until they see someone who looked exactly like them, same gap, same fear, and made it through. That story does more than any badge ever could, because it makes the outcome feel real instead of theoretical. Once they feel genuinely seen and understood, they're ready to trust someone who plainly knows how re-entry works, but that warmth has to come first or the expertise doesn't work on them.
prose_plain.push: They've been out long enough that the fear of going back has grown bigger than the discomfort of staying out, and the anxiety about walking into an office again feels almost physical.
prose_plain.pull: They're looking for proof that someone in their exact situation found a way to feel ready, and they want a clear path that shows them how to get there too.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're afraid employers will write them off the moment they see the gap, and they're also afraid a new job will turn into another traumatic experience, and underneath both of those is a quieter fear that they're just not ready yet.
prose_plain.habit: They keep telling themselves they need a little more time before they start applying, so they stay out longer, skip the job boards, and wait for a feeling of readiness that doesn't seem to come on its own.

prose_plain.t1_name: They want their body to keep going

prose_plain.t5_name: They don't believe patience works

prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'slow down and build your base' so many times it's become noise. They tried it, and the breathlessness didn't go away, so that advice is dead to them. Now they treat anything that sounds like a variation of patience as proof that the person talking doesn't actually understand what's happening in their body.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're not moved by enthusiasm or transformation promises because they've already heard those and they didn't pan out. What shifts them is badges tied specifically to breathing and aerobic capacity, because that tells them the person knows what's actually failing. And when they read about another runner who described the same gasping wall and then went from short runs to long ones, that story works harder than any claim a coach could make about themselves.
prose_plain.push: They can't get enough air even when they slow right down, and that wall keeps ending their runs before they're ready to stop.
prose_plain.pull: They believe their body can handle more distance if they can just get the breathing sorted, and they're not ready to give up on that.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if slowing down doesn't even help, something is broken in their lungs or their fitness that no amount of training will ever fix.
prose_plain.habit: When breathing gets hard, they slow down because that's the obvious move, but it hasn't worked and they keep doing it anyway because they don't know what else to try.

prose_plain.implication: They've heard 'slow down and build your base' so many times it's stopped meaning anything. They tried it, the breathlessness didn't go away, and now any advice that sounds like a version of that same thing gets ignored before it's finished. They're not looking for encouragement or a longer version of what they already know. They want an actual explanation for why their breathing hits a wall.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust enthusiasm because they're chasing a performance outcome, not a feeling, and good vibes don't get someone to a finish line. badges that connect directly to breathing and aerobic capacity tell them this person knows the specific thing that's broken. Hearing from another runner who described the same gasping problem and then went from three miles to ten miles is more convincing than any promise, because it tells them the problem is solvable and someone like them solved it.
prose_plain.push: They can't get enough air even when they slow right down, and that wall keeps cutting their runs short before they get anywhere near the distance they're training for.
prose_plain.pull: They want to keep adding distance, and they believe their body should be able to do it if they can just sort out what's going wrong with their breathing.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that if slowing down doesn't even help, something is fundamentally broken in their fitness or their lungs, and training harder or longer won't change that.
prose_plain.habit: When breathing gets hard they slow down because that's the obvious thing to do, but it hasn't fixed anything and they keep going back to it anyway because they don't have another answer yet.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Close complex deals and hit quota every quarter
prose_plain.note: This buyer lives and breathes enterprise sales. They already know the basics. What they want is help with the hard part: keeping multiple decision-makers moving in the same direction across a long, slow sales cycle. Generic sales advice bores them.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want to win deals and keep the money
prose_plain.t2_name: Lost deals and shrinking margins hurt
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to close without feeling dirty
prose_plain.t4_name: They think it'll make them pushy
prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried every method already
prose_plain.t6_name: They trust someone who sold for real
prose_plain.implication: They've been through MEDDIC, Challenger, and every variation of 'handle the objection and ask for the sale.' Each time, it either felt manipulative in the room or it blew up and the client went cold. So they've stopped believing that any method fixes the thing underneath, which is the fear that selling and manipulating are the same thing.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't listen to someone who hasn't actually lived inside a sales room and hit quota there, so real-world authority is what gets them to pay attention at all. Once they're paying attention, they need to see people who look exactly like them closing deals without cutting price, because that's the only proof that it's possible for someone in their position. They're also already wired to follow a process step by step, so when a method asks them to commit to small actions and stack wins one on top of the other, it fits the way they already think about getting better.
prose_plain.push: They're losing deals they should be winning, their margins are shrinking every time they cave and drop the price, and the rejection has started to feel personal enough that they dread picking up the phone.
prose_plain.pull: They want to get to yes without pushing, without apologising, and without shaving money off the deal just to stop feeling uncomfortable. They want to hit their number and feel okay about how they got there.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're worried that any new approach will just turn them into a slicker version of the pushy salesperson they already hate, or that they'll try it and still get rejected and still cave on price anyway.
prose_plain.habit: They drop the price the moment a prospect hesitates, and they've mostly stopped doing cold outreach because the silence or the no feels worse than just working the warm leads they already have.

They've sat through enough training promises that they've stopped believing the method is the problem, because they've tried the methods. What they've decided is that something is broken in them specifically, and that's a much harder thing to be sold a fix for.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't slow down for a coach who hasn't clearly lived inside a real sales room and hit a real number there, because their radar for people who only teach sales without having done it is sharp and unforgiving. Once a coach earns that credibility, they need to see people who look like them, same market, same deals, same fear of discounting, coming out the other side hitting quota without cutting prices, because that's the only evidence that it's actually possible for someone in their exact situation. They're also already wired to improve step by step and track what they're doing differently, so a method that builds on small committed actions fits the way they already think about getting better at their job.
prose_plain.push: They're losing deals they should've won, their margins shrink every time a prospect hesitates and they fold on price, and the rejection has gotten personal enough that picking up the phone now feels like something to avoid.
prose_plain.pull: They want to get to yes without pushing, without apologising, and without shaving money off the deal just to make the awkward silence stop. They want to hit their number and feel decent about how they got there.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're worried that whatever they try next will just turn them into a shinier version of the pushy salesperson they already hate, or that they'll do everything right and still get rejected and still cave when it counts.
prose_plain.habit: They drop the price the moment a prospect hesitates, and they've mostly stopped doing cold outreach because the silence or the no feels worse than staying safe with the warm leads they already have.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me use self-compassion to stand up for myself and set limits, not just feel better.

prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried this and it didn't stick
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's been in it
prose_plain.implication: They've heard about self-compassion. They've read about it, probably practiced it in therapy, and felt genuine relief for a moment before the self-hatred came crashing back. Because it's slipped away so many times, they don't trust that understanding the idea is the same as being able to use it when it counts.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They can tell immediately when someone sounds clinical and far away, and that distance makes them feel more alone, not less. They're often carrying real diagnoses and are in active therapy, so they're checking whether the person in front of them actually knows what they're dealing with. And more than almost anything else, they need to hear that someone else felt this stuck and got through it, because that's the only thing they can actually believe right now.
prose_plain.push: They've spent years feeling useless and embarrassed, and even therapy sessions sometimes leave them hating themselves more than when they walked in.
prose_plain.pull: They want to stop punishing themselves, forgive themselves for things they can't let go of, and actually believe that getting better is possible for them.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this is just who they are, that the self-hatred is permanent, and that if therapy hasn't fixed it then nothing will.
prose_plain.habit: When something goes wrong, their first move is to turn on themselves, and that reflex kicks in automatically, even after sessions where they felt like they'd made real progress.

prose_plain.t3_name: They want to feel like they can keep going

prose_plain.t5_name: They've tried self-compassion and lost it
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's actually been there
prose_plain.implication: They've heard about self-compassion. They've probably read about it, talked about it in therapy, and felt something shift for a moment before the self-hatred came back harder than before. Because it hasn't stuck, they don't believe that understanding the idea is the same as being able to live it, and they're tired of being handed something that sounds right but falls apart the second things get hard.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They can tell immediately when someone is talking at them from a distance, and that distance makes them feel more alone, not less. They're carrying real diagnoses and are often already in therapy, so they're checking whether whoever is in front of them actually knows what that's like from the inside. And what they're really hoping to find is proof that someone felt exactly this stuck and came out the other side, because that's the only thing that makes getting better feel real to them.
prose_plain.push: They've spent years feeling useless and embarrassed, and even therapy sessions can leave them hating themselves more than when they walked in.
prose_plain.pull: They want to stop punishing themselves, forgive themselves for things they can't let go of, and feel like getting better is actually possible for them.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared this is just how they are, that the self-hatred is permanent, and that if therapy hasn't fixed it nothing will.
prose_plain.habit: When something goes wrong, their first move is to turn on themselves, and that reflex kicks in automatically, even after sessions where they felt some progress.

They're also relieved when they find out other people felt exactly this broken and got better, because their biggest fear is that their body is the one exception that can't be fixed. And when someone explains the real reason they feel this way before asking for anything, they feel seen rather than sold to, which is the only reason they keep reading.

They tried it, stared at the page, wrote two sentences, and walked away convinced the problem was them, not the advice. prose_plain.cialdini_why: They won't trust the practice until someone with real badges, a therapist or a researcher, says it's been studied and it holds up, because their own experience already told them it didn't work. And because they've quit before, even a small step they choose to take on their own pulls them forward, since going back on their own word feels worse than carrying on.
prose_plain.push: They're sitting on feelings they haven't sorted out and they don't know where to put them. Sometimes they don't even know what they'd write down first, and that confusion is enough to stop them before they've picked up a pen.

prose_plain.t3_name: They want proof recovery actually happens

And when they find someone whose story sounds like theirs, it's the first real evidence they've had that recovery isn't something that only happens to other people.
prose_plain.push: They're having vivid flashbacks that yank them out of the present, and they're doing it alone because the people closest to them say the pain isn't real. They haven't found a single tool that reliably helps when things get bad.
prose_plain.pull: They want something that gives them actual relief right now, and they want to see real people with C-PTSD who recovered, not just learned to cope better.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that what happened to them is too complicated or too severe to ever get better, and that they're the one person recovery won't work for.

prose_plain.note: These buyers have been hurt by the work itself, not just tired by it. They respond to coaches who know this world from the inside, and to seeing others in the same profession say it helped them.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their body to work again
prose_plain.t2_name: Rest stopped doing anything
prose_plain.t3_name: They want to keep caring without collapsing
prose_plain.t4_name: They can't leave the job draining them
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing rest fixes it
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's seen it heal
prose_plain.implication: They've already done everything a reasonable person tries first. Sleep, time off, weekends away, cutting stimulants, all of it, and the exhaustion was still there on Monday morning. So when they hear words like 'self-care' or 'rest more,' they don't just tune it out, they actively distrust the person saying it, because those words belong to a road they've already walked to the end.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're not looking for someone who sounds credentialed or clinical, they're looking for someone who has genuinely watched people come back from this, because their own experience has given them real reasons to doubt it's possible. Hearing from others who were in the same kind of exhaustion and got through it is the only thing that makes hope feel honest rather than naive. They're depleted and wary, so they won't warm to anyone who feels distant or preachy, they need to feel felt before they'll feel any trust.
prose_plain.push: They've worked hard for a long time and now the tiredness doesn't lift even after real rest, and that frightens them in a way they can't explain away.
prose_plain.pull: They want to hear from someone who actually came back from this level of burnout, and they want an honest account of how long it took and what actually changed.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that nothing will work because rest already failed them, and they can't walk away from the job that's doing this to them.
prose_plain.habit: They keep showing up to the same job, resting passively on weekends, and waiting to feel better on their own, even though that cycle hasn't broken in a long time.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Actually heal and get their strength back after a breakdown, before they even think about going back to work.
prose_plain.note: These people have already hit the wall hard. They know exactly what happened to them and they aren't interested in pushing through. They want real recovery first, full stop.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want their body to work again
prose_plain.t2_name: Rest stopped doing anything
prose_plain.t3_name: They want proof someone actually healed
prose_plain.t4_name: They can't leave the job draining them
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing rest fixes it
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's seen it heal
prose_plain.implication: They've already done the things everyone told them to do. Sleep, holidays, weekends off, less caffeine, and none of it touched what's underneath. So when they hear anything that sounds like 'rest more' or 'take care of yourself,' they don't just tune it out, they actively distrust whoever's saying it, because those words have already failed them in the real world.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They're not short on information, they're short on evidence that this actually gets better, because their own body has given them real reasons to doubt it. Hearing from people who came back from the same kind of collapse is the only thing that makes hope feel honest rather than naive. And because they're depleted and wary, they won't warm to someone who sounds clinical or detached, they need to feel like the person talking has genuinely been close to this kind of exhaustion.
prose_plain.push: They worked hard for too long and now nothing they try makes a dent in the exhaustion, and that frightens them.
prose_plain.pull: They want to hear how someone actually healed from serious burnout, and how long it honestly took.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that nothing will work because rest already failed them, and they can't walk away from the job that's still draining them.
prose_plain.habit: They keep pushing through the same job, resting passively on weekends, and waiting to feel better on their own.

prose_plain.jtbd_job: Help me get my thesis or papers finished and published so I keep my position and move forward in my career.
prose_plain.note: These writers aren't writing for love of it. They're writing because their job depends on it. That's a very different pressure from someone who wants to write a book.
prose_plain.t1_name: They want proof they can finish
prose_plain.t2_name: Self-doubt got loud enough to stop them
prose_plain.t3_name: They want a manuscript they're proud of
prose_plain.t4_name: They're scared finishing will confirm the worst
prose_plain.t5_name: They've stopped believing advice will help
prose_plain.t6_name: They need someone who's actually done it
prose_plain.implication: They've been told to show up every day, track their word counts, join the writing challenge, and just keep going. Every one of those things worked for a few days and then stalled, and now the advice sounds like background noise. They're not looking for another system, they're looking for someone whose finished book proves that people like them actually get to the end.
prose_plain.cialdini_why: They don't trust their own judgement about their writing right now, so they look for someone outside themselves to borrow confidence from. A coach who has published a book signals that finishing isn't a personality trait they're missing, it's something real and learnable. And when they see other stuck, doubting writers who crossed the finish line, it gets harder to hold onto the story that they're the one person this won't work for.
prose_plain.push: They're in the middle of a project they care about, and the self-doubt has gotten loud enough that they can't make themselves open the file.
prose_plain.pull: They want to move forward consistently and end up with a finished manuscript they actually feel good about.
prose_plain.anxiety: They're scared that finishing the book will just prove the voice in their head right, that nobody will read it and they were never a real writer.
prose_plain.habit: They wait until they feel ready or inspired, and because that feeling rarely shows up when they need it, weeks go by without a word on the page.
